name: The I Ching — All Lenses (meta)
description: Every I Ching grammar in this repo, read together. One composite item per hexagram gathers its item from each lens: the trigrams and the Great Image as scenery, Legge's text, the Human Design reading as what the hexagram asks of a person, the book chapter as story, the repair reading as wound. A cast path through these is a spread; its story is what emerges from the composites it passes through.

sections.Scenery: Heaven over Heaven. Heaven, in its motion, (gives the idea of) strength. The superior man, in accordance with this, nerves himself to ceaseless activity.
sections.Text: Khien (represents) what is great and originating, penetrating, advantageous, correct and firm.
sections.What it asks: Creative Power. Gate 1 represents the archetypal force of creative self-expression and unique direction. This is the impulse to express something that only you can bring into the world. In the bodygraph, it sits in the G Center (Identity) and speaks to knowing your creative direction in life, your unique contribution, your authentic voice. When this gate is defined (activated by planets at birth), there may be a consistent pull toward expressing individuality and showing others new directions or possibilities. When undefined, there's more flexibility about creative direction, sampling different paths without fixed commitment. The classical I Ching interpretation emphasizes pure creative power—heaven doubled—suggesting relentless forward motion and the ability to initiate cycles. In Human Design's reinterpretation, this becomes personal creative authority rather than cosmic force. The energy here is about demonstrating that each person has a unique direction to offer, modeling individuality without demanding that others follow. The shadow appears when creativity is forced on demand, when expression becomes performative rather than authentic, or when the need to be unique overrides genuine self-knowing. The gift is natural self-expression that inspires without coercion—you show what's possible simply by being yourself creatively. Practically, this gate often manifests as people looking to you for creative direction, not because you're trying to lead but because your authentic expression naturally reveals new possibilities. This is symbolic language for contemplating your relationship to creative individuality, not a fixed mandate about who you must be.

sections.Scenery: Earth over Earth. The (capacity and sustaining) power of the earth is what is denoted by Khwăn. The superior man, in accordance with this, with his large virtue supports (men and) things.
sections.Text: Khwăn (represents) what is great and originating, penetrating, advantageous, correct and having the firmness of a mare. When the superior man (here intended) has to make any movement, if he take the initiative, he will go astray; if he follow, he will find his (proper) lord. The advantageousness will be seen in his getting friends in the south-west, and losing friends in the north-east. If he rest in correctness and firmness, there will be good fortune.
sections.What it asks: Receptive Flow. Gate 2 represents receptive knowing of direction—the counterpart to Gate 1's creative expression. This is your connection to intuitive guidance about where you're meant to go, your internal GPS for life direction. When defined, there's consistent access to inner knowing about direction. When undefined, direction is sampled from others and learned through experience. The classical I Ching's pure receptivity—earth doubled—emphasizes yielding strength, the power of allowing rather than forcing. In Human Design's framework, this becomes your capacity to receive direction from something larger than ego: intuition, higher self, synchronicity, whatever language fits your worldview. The key distinction is that this isn't passive waiting; it's responsive receptivity. You know where you're going by staying open to intuitive hits, dreams, gut feelings, or simply allowing the knowing to emerge rather than manufacturing it mentally. The shadow is forcing direction through willpower when genuine inner knowing isn't present, or spiritual bypassing where you avoid responsibility by waiting for the universe to tell you everything. The gift is trusting receptive knowing even when it doesn't make logical sense, even when you can't explain why you're going this direction. Practically, this gate often manifests as finding that your best direction comes when you stop trying to figure it out mentally and just allow the knowing to surface. Whether this reflects actual energetic wiring or is simply a useful metaphor for trusting intuition over analysis is an open question. The archetypal language can be valuable for contemplation regardless.

sections.Scenery: Water over Thunder. (The trigram representing) clouds and (that representing) thunder form Kun. The superior man, in accordance with this, (adjusts his measures of government) as in sorting the threads of the warp and woof.
sections.Text: Kun (indicates that in the case which it presupposes) there will be great progress and success, and the advantage will come from being correct and firm. (But) any movement in advance should not be (lightly) undertaken. There will be advantage in appointing feudal princes.
sections.What it asks: Difficulty at the Beginning. Gate 3 in the Sacral Center represents mutation or ordering through chaos—the energy of innovation through experimentation. This is about starting new things even when you don't have all the pieces figured out, trusting that order will emerge from the initial chaos. The classical hexagram speaks to the difficulty inherent in all beginnings: thunder and water mixing creates turbulence before clarity. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes your relationship to change, novelty, and the messy process of bringing new things into form. If defined, there's consistent access to innovative energy, though it may feel chaotic or uncertain. You can handle disorder because you trust that patterns will emerge. If undefined, innovation comes in bursts or is learned from others. The shadow is forcing change just for change's sake, getting addicted to chaos, or getting stuck in perpetual experimentation without bringing things to completion. The gift is trusting the mutation process—knowing that difficulty at the beginning doesn't mean you're on the wrong path, it just means you're actually creating something new rather than repeating the known. Order emerges through the experimental process, not before it. Practically, this gate often manifests as being pulled toward experimental approaches, struggling with traditional orderly systems, and excelling when given permission to try unusual solutions. Whether this reflects actual energetic design or is simply a useful lens for understanding different approaches to innovation and change remains contemplative territory. The archetypal language serves self-reflection.

sections.Scenery: Mountain over Water. (The trigram representing) a mountain, and beneath it that for a spring issuing forth form Măng. The superior man, in accordance with this, strives to be resolute in his conduct and nourishes his virtue.
sections.Text: Măng (indicates that in the case which it presupposes) there will be progress and success. I do not (go and) seek the youthful and inexperienced, but he comes and seeks me. When he shows (the sincerity that marks) the first recourse to divination, I instruct him. If he apply a second and third time, that is troublesome; and I do not instruct the troublesome. There will be advantage in being firm and correct.
sections.What it asks: Youthful Folly. Gate 4 in the Ajna Center represents the process of forming mental formulas, answers, and logical frameworks. This is about your relationship to mental certainty and conceptual organization. In the classical I Ching, 'youthful folly' refers to the inexperienced mind that asks questions without yet understanding how to evaluate answers. In Human Design's reinterpretation, this becomes whether you have consistent access to mental clarity and formulization. If defined, there's a reliable way of arriving at conclusions and creating frameworks. You might be the person others come to for answers. If undefined, thinking is more fluid and open to multiple perspectives without needing certainty. The classical wisdom here is about respecting the process of learning: don't ask the same question repeatedly expecting different answers. Form your answer, test it, revise it based on results. The shadow is either getting stuck in rigid mental formulas ('this IS the answer') or drowning in uncertainty because you can't commit to any framework. The gift is mental clarity that serves others—not because your formulas are objectively correct, but because they're coherent enough to be useful. Your frameworks help organize complexity into workable patterns. Practically, this gate often manifests as naturally systematizing information, creating frameworks, or developing formulas (mathematical, philosophical, practical) that help make sense of complex data. Remember that this speaks to mental processing style, not intelligence or correctness. Different ways of thinking have different gifts.

sections.Scenery: Water over Heaven. (The trigram for) clouds ascending over that for the sky forms Hsü. The superior man, in accordance with this, eats and drinks, feasts and enjoys himself (as if there were nothing else to employ him).
sections.Text: Hsü intimates that, with the sincerity which is declared in it, there will be brilliant success. With firmness there will be good fortune; and it will be advantageous to cross the great stream.
sections.What it asks: Waiting. Gate 5 in the Sacral Center represents fixed rhythms and natural patterns of consistency. This is about your relationship to habit, routine, and regular patterns in life. The classical I Ching hexagram emphasizes waiting with confidence—not anxious waiting, but patient trust that the right timing will emerge. Water above heaven suggests nourishment that will come in its natural time. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes about your body's natural rhythms: sleep, hunger, work cycles, creative flow. If this gate is defined in your Sacral, there's a consistent daily rhythm that works well—disrupting it causes depletion. You might naturally wake at the same time, need meals at regular intervals, or have predictable energy patterns. If undefined, there's more flexibility with timing and rhythms, adapting easily to changing schedules. The shadow is rigidity—forcing yourself or others to conform to a fixed pattern even when life requires flexibility. Or conversely, fighting against your natural rhythms because they seem boring or limiting. The gift is honoring consistent patterns without making them an identity or prison. You can have a morning routine and still adapt when needed. The structure serves you; you don't serve the structure. Practically, this gate often manifests as thriving with regular schedules and predictability. Travel, irregular hours, or chaos might be more depleting than for others. Whether this reflects actual energetic wiring or is a useful framework for understanding individual differences in need for consistency versus variety remains an open question for contemplation.

sections.Scenery: Heaven over Water. (The trigram representing) heaven and (that representing) water, moving away from each other, form Sung. The superior man, in accordance with this, in the transaction of affairs takes good counsel about his first steps.
sections.Text: Sung intimates how, though there is sincerity in one's contention, he will yet meet with opposition and obstruction; but if he cherish an apprehensive caution, there will be good fortune, while, if he must prosecute the contention to the (bitter) end, there will be evil. It will be advantageous to see the great man; it will not be advantageous to cross the great stream.
sections.What it asks: Conflict. Gate 6 in the Solar Plexus Center represents friction in intimacy—the necessary negotiation that happens when two people (or parts of yourself) have different emotional truths. This isn't conflict for conflict's sake, but the honest friction required to find authentic alignment. The classical hexagram shows heaven and water moving in opposite directions, suggesting inherent tension. In Human Design's reading, this becomes about emotional negotiation: how do you handle friction in intimate relationships? If defined in your emotional solar plexus, there's consistent energy for working through emotional friction. You might actually be comfortable with conflict as a doorway to deeper intimacy. If undefined, you might avoid friction or feel overwhelmed by emotional tension. The shadow is either forcing conflict unnecessarily (friction addiction) or suppressing genuine friction and pretending everything is fine. Neither extreme serves intimacy. The gift is recognizing that friction is how intimate systems find authentic alignment—not through pretending to agree, but through honest negotiation of different truths. You're willing to experience the discomfort of disagreement because you trust it leads somewhere real. Practically, this gate often manifests as close relationships involving substantial honest conflict. You might say 'we fight a lot but we're really close' and mean it positively. The friction builds intimacy rather than destroying it. The challenge is distinguishing productive friction (leading to deeper understanding) from destructive conflict (just causing harm). This is contemplative territory for exploring your relationship to emotional honesty in intimacy.

sections.Wound: Chapter 1 of the Repair book asks: what if 69% of problems never get solved? Hexagram 6 is the I Ching's answer. Conflict arises not from error but from structure. Heaven and Water are not enemies — they simply have different natures. The judgment says: 'It is advantageous to see the great man. It is not advantageous to cross the great water.' Translation: seek mediation. Don't escalate. The problem is perpetual. The repair is in how you hold it.

sections.Scenery: Earth over Water. (The trigram representing) the earth and in the midst of it that representing water, form Sze. The superior man, in accordance with this, nourishes and educates the people, and collects (from among them) the multitudes (of the hosts).
sections.Text: Sze indicates how, in the case which it supposes, with firmness and correctness, and (a leader of) age and experience, there will be good fortune and no error.
sections.What it asks: The Army. Gate 7 in the G Center represents your role in leading or influencing others. The classical I Ching uses military metaphor: an army requires clear direction and responsible leadership. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes about your identity in relation to others—what role do you naturally play in collective settings? Are you a director, a guide, a democratic leader, or someone who prefers not to lead at all? If this gate is defined, there's consistent energy for taking a role in influencing or directing others. People might naturally look to you for guidance or expect you to take charge. If undefined, you're more flexible about roles and might not feel called to lead. The shadow is either forcing yourself into leadership when it's not your natural expression, or abdicating all responsibility for influence when you actually do have something valuable to contribute. The gift is recognizing that leadership isn't about domination; it's about clear direction that serves the collective. You know your role, you play it well, and you don't inflate or deflate its importance. You lead when appropriate and follow when appropriate, without making either an identity. Practically, this gate often manifests as finding yourself in guiding roles—not necessarily formal authority, but informal influence. You're the friend everyone comes to for direction, the colleague who naturally organizes projects, the family member who provides orientation. This is contemplative territory for exploring your relationship to influence and collective roles.

sections.Scenery: Water over Earth. (The trigram representing) the earth, and over it (that representing) water, form Pî. The ancient kings, in accordance with this, established the various states and maintained an affectionate relation to their princes.
sections.Text: Pî indicates that (under the conditions which it supposes) there is good fortune. But let (the principal party intended in it) re-examine himself, (as if) by divination, whether his virtue be great, unintermitting, and firm. If it be so, there will be no error. Those who have not rest will then come to him; and with those who are (too) late in coming it will be ill.
sections.What it asks: Holding Together. Gate 8 in the Throat Center represents contribution through authentic self-expression and modeling. This is about whether you make your unique contribution by demonstrating what's possible through your own example. The classical I Ching hexagram emphasizes union and holding together—water on earth creates cohesion. In Human Design's reinterpretation, this becomes about your relationship to being a role model or example. If this gate is defined in your Throat (the center of manifestation and expression), there's consistent energy for contributing by being yourself authentically and letting others learn from what you model. You're not teaching directly; you're inspiring by example. If undefined, you might contribute in other ways or be more private about your process. The shadow is performing authenticity (trying to be a role model without actually being authentic), or hiding your gifts because you don't want the visibility that comes with modeling. The gift is realizing that your authentic expression naturally contributes to the collective—you don't have to force it or manufacture it. When you're genuinely yourself, others learn something simply from witnessing your unique way of being. You contribute through honest self-expression, not through trying to set an example. Practically, this gate often manifests as feeling energized by visibility and authenticity, even when uncomfortable. You might be the friend whose honesty gives others permission to be honest, or the colleague whose unique approach opens possibilities for the team. The contemplative question is about your relationship to visibility, modeling, and contribution through authentic being.

items.name: 9 · The Taming Power of the Small

sections.Scenery: Wind over Heaven. (The trigram representing) the sky, and that representing wind moving above it, form Hsiâo Khû The superior man, in accordance with this, adorns the outward manifestation of his virtue.
sections.Text: Hsiâo Khû indicates that (under its conditions) there will be progress and success. (We see) dense clouds, but no rain coming from our borders in the west.
sections.What it asks: Taming Power of the Small. Gate 9 in the Sacral Center represents the power of focus on details—the capacity to concentrate life force energy on small, specific elements that accumulate into larger patterns. This isn't about missing the forest for the trees; it's about recognizing that forests are made of individual trees, each deserving attention. The classical hexagram shows wind gathering clouds without yet producing rain—potential building through patient accumulation of small elements. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes your relationship to detailed focus: can you sustain attention on specifics without losing sight of the whole? If this gate is defined in your Sacral, there's consistent energy for detailed work. You might be the person who notices what others miss, who can work with sustained attention on seemingly minor elements, who finds meaning in precision. If undefined, your focus tends toward the general or big picture, learning about detail orientation from others. The shadow appears when detail focus becomes perfectionism, when attention to small things masks avoidance of larger challenges, or when you get so lost in specifics that synthesis becomes impossible. The gift is precision that serves purpose—you can zoom in without losing perspective, attend to particulars while maintaining awareness of how they fit into wholes. You recognize that breakthrough often emerges from careful attention to what seems small rather than grasping for the dramatic. Practically, this gate often manifests as natural ability for detailed work, enjoyment of tasks others find tedious, and capacity to find patterns in specifics. Whether this reflects actual energetic wiring or is useful metaphor for different cognitive styles remains contemplative territory.

sections.Scenery: Heaven over Lake. (The trigram representing) the sky above, and below it (that representing the waters of) a marsh, form Lî. The superior man, in accordance with this, discriminates between high and low, and gives settlement to the aims of the people.
sections.Text: (Lî suggests the idea of) one treading on the tail of a tiger, which does not bite him. There will be progress and success.
sections.What it asks: Treading. Gate 10 in the G Center represents behavior of the self—how you naturally conduct yourself in the world, your authentic way of being that comes from self-love rather than performance. The classical hexagram suggests treading carefully in dangerous places, walking the tiger's tail without getting bitten through proper conduct. In Human Design's framework, this becomes about whether your behavior flows from genuine self-acceptance or from trying to be what you think you should be. If this gate is defined in your G Center, there's consistent energy for authentic self-conduct. You might be someone who naturally behaves in ways that feel true to yourself, even when unconventional. Your behavior isn't calculated for effect; it emerges from self-love. If undefined, your behavior is more flexible and adaptive, learning different modes of conduct from various situations and people. The shadow appears when behavior becomes performance—when you're so focused on conducting yourself 'correctly' that authenticity disappears, or when self-love hardens into narcissism where only your way is valid. The gift is natural authenticity—your behavior reflects genuine self-acceptance, which paradoxically makes it easier for others to be authentic around you. You tread carefully not from fear but from respect for both yourself and others. You can be fully yourself without trampling on others' right to be themselves. Practically, this gate often shows up as people saying 'you're always so yourself' or 'I can be myself around you.' Whether this reflects energetic design or useful language for self-acceptance remains open for contemplation.

sections.Scenery: Earth over Heaven. (The trigrams for) heaven and earth in communication together form Thâi. The (sage) sovereign, in harmony with this, fashions and completes (his regulations) after the courses of heaven and earth, and assists the application of the adaptations furnished by them,—in order to benefit the people.
sections.Text: In Thâi (we see) the little gone and the great come. (It indicates that) there will be good fortune, with progress and success.
sections.What it asks: Peace. Gate 11 in the Ajna Center represents ideas and concepts—the mental capacity to receive and generate abstract thoughts that may or may not have immediate practical application. The classical hexagram shows heaven and earth in harmonious union, suggesting that peace emerges when higher and lower, abstract and concrete, find alignment. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes your relationship to ideas: do you have consistent access to conceptual thinking, or is your mind more focused on immediate practical matters? If this gate is defined in your Ajna, there's regular energy for idea generation. You might be someone who has lots of ideas, who lives partly in the realm of concepts, who can think abstractly with ease. People might come to you for new perspectives or unusual angles. If undefined, your thinking is more grounded in what's immediately relevant, learning about abstract ideation from others. The shadow is either idea addiction (so many concepts that nothing gets implemented) or getting lost in mental realms disconnected from embodied reality. The gift is idea generation that serves life—you can think conceptually without losing touch with what matters on the ground. Your ideas create peace rather than confusion because they help people see new possibilities without demanding they abandon practical wisdom. Practically, this gate often manifests as being 'the idea person' in groups, having insights that seem to come from nowhere, or finding that your best contribution is conceptual rather than implementation-focused. This is contemplative territory for exploring how abstract thinking serves lived experience.

sections.Wound: Chapter 10 is 'Re-Pairing' — the culminating practice of turning toward each other, toward the earth, toward the cosmos. Hexagram 11 is what that looks like in the I Ching: Heaven and Earth approaching each other. Not stasis — communion. The judgment says: 'Peace. The small departs, the great approaches. Good fortune. Success.' In Gottman's terms: the repair attempt lands. In Johnson's: the vulnerability request is received. In Akomolafe's: the crack opens into a garden. In the I Ching's: Earth descends and Heaven rises and they meet in the middle, which is where all life happens — in the middle. Not above. Not below. In the meeting.

sections.Scenery: Heaven over Earth. (The trigrams of) heaven and earth, not in intercommunication, form Phî. The superior man, in accordance with this, restrains (the manifestation of) his virtue, and avoids the calamities (that threaten him). There is no opportunity of conferring on him the glory of emolument.
sections.Text: In Phî there is the want of good understanding between the (different classes of) men, and its indication is unfavourable to the firm and correct course of the superior man. We see in it the great gone and the little come.
sections.What it asks: Standstill. Gate 12 in the Throat Center represents caution in expression—knowing when to speak and when to remain silent, when to articulate what you know and when to wait for right timing. The classical hexagram shows heaven and earth separated, communication blocked, suggesting that sometimes standstill is the appropriate response rather than forced movement. In Human Design's reading, this becomes your relationship to expressing yourself: do you have consistent access to knowing when to speak versus when to pause? If this gate is defined in your Throat, there's regular energy for discerning right timing of expression. You might be someone who knows when words will land versus when they'll fall on deaf ears, who can hold back expression when the moment isn't ripe. If undefined, your expression is more spontaneous or learned situationally from others. The shadow appears when caution becomes suppression (never speaking up) or when timing-awareness becomes manipulation (withholding strategically for effect). The gift is wise restraint that serves communication—you know that not everything that can be said should be said, and not every moment is the right moment. Your caution isn't fear; it's respect for the power of words and awareness of readiness in listeners. Practically, this gate often manifests as being told 'you always know the right time to say things' or finding that when you do speak after waiting, people really hear you. This is contemplative territory about the relationship between silence and speech.

sections.Scenery: Heaven over Fire. (The trigrams for) heaven and fire form Thung Zăn. The superior man, in accordance with this, distinguishes things according to their kinds and classes.
sections.Text: Thung Zăn (or 'Union of men') appears here (as we find it) in the (remote districts of the) country, indicating progress and success. It will be advantageous to cross the great stream. It will be advantageous to maintain the firm correctness of the superior man.
sections.What it asks: Fellowship. Gate 13 in the G Center represents the listener—the capacity to hear and hold others' stories, secrets, and experiences, to serve as witness to what people need to express. The classical hexagram emphasizes fellowship in the open, suggesting that genuine community emerges when people can share openly with those who truly listen. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes whether you have consistent energy for deep listening and holding space for others' expression. If this gate is defined in your G Center, there's regular capacity for listening without needing to fix, judge, or redirect. You might be the person people naturally confide in, who can hear difficult truths without collapsing or rejecting. Your listening creates fellowship because people feel genuinely met. If undefined, you learn about deep listening from others and may be more focused on your own expression. The shadow appears when listening becomes passive reception without boundaries, when you're so busy holding others' stories that you lose your own voice, or when 'being a good listener' becomes an identity that prevents authentic relationship. The gift is generative listening—your capacity to hear others actually helps them hear themselves. You don't just receive; your listening creates space for people to discover what they really need to say. Practically, this gate often shows up as 'I don't know why I'm telling you this' or people feeling understood in your presence. This is contemplative territory about the power of being witnessed.

sections.Scenery: Fire over Heaven. (The trigram for) heaven and (that of) fire above it form Tâ Yû The superior man, in accordance with this, represses what is evil and gives distinction to what is good, in sympathy with the excellent Heaven-conferred (nature).
sections.Text: Tâ Yû indicates that, (under the circumstances which it implies), there will be great progress and success.
sections.What it asks: Possession in Great Measure. Gate 14 in the Sacral Center represents power skills—the capacity to develop and wield resources, whether material, energetic, or skillful, and to do so in service of something meaningful. The classical hexagram shows fire in heaven, suggesting that true possession comes from alignment with higher purpose rather than mere accumulation. In Human Design's reading, this becomes your relationship to power and resources: do you have consistent energy for building skills and resources? If this gate is defined in your Sacral, there's regular life force available for developing mastery, for accumulating what's needed, for building capacity over time. You might be someone who naturally gets good at things, who can sustain effort toward skill development, who knows how to marshal resources. If undefined, your relationship to power and skills is more situational, learning from others about mastery. The shadow appears when possession becomes hoarding, when power is accumulated for its own sake rather than for service, or when skill development disconnects from purpose. The gift is empowered service—you develop power and skills specifically to serve something beyond yourself. Your resources empower others rather than creating dependency or envy. Practically, this gate often manifests as natural capacity for skill acquisition, comfort with power when it serves purpose, and ability to translate resources into action. This is contemplative territory about the relationship between power and service.

sections.Scenery: Earth over Mountain. (The trigram for) the earth and (that of) a mountain in the midst of it form Khien. The superior man, in accordance with this, diminishes what is excessive (in himself), and increases where there is any defect, bringing about an equality, according to the nature of the case, in his treatment (of himself and others).
sections.Text: Khien indicates progress and success. The superior man, (being humble as it implies), will have a (good) issue (to his undertakings).
sections.What it asks: Modesty. Gate 15 in the G Center represents extremes—the capacity to experience the full range from high to low, abundance to scarcity, ecstasy to despair, and to find modesty (right relationship) with these extremes rather than identifying with them. The classical hexagram shows a mountain beneath earth, suggesting that true power lies in humility rather than display. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes your relationship to rhythm and extremes: do you naturally move through highs and lows with equanimity, or do extremes destabilize you? If this gate is defined in your G Center, there's consistent energy for riding life's waves without getting lost in either peak or valley. You might be someone who can hold both extremes simultaneously, who knows prosperity and scarcity are temporary, who remains human through all conditions. If undefined, you experience extremes more dramatically or learn about balance from others. The shadow appears when you identify with extremes (becoming manic or depressive rather than experiencing moods), when modesty becomes false humility or self-diminishment, or when balancing extremes means never fully experiencing either. The gift is genuine modesty—you can be extraordinary without losing your humanity, can experience abundance without superiority or scarcity without shame. You know that extremes are natural rhythms, not definitions of worth. Practically, this gate often shows up as resilience through life's ups and downs, capacity to remain grounded during success or failure. This is contemplative territory about identity beyond circumstance.

sections.Scenery: Thunder over Earth. (The trigrams for) the earth and thunder issuing from it with its crashing noise form Yü. The ancient kings, in accordance with this, composed their music and did honour to virtue, presenting it especially and most grandly to God, when they associated with Him (at the service) their highest ancestor and their father.
sections.Text: Yü indicates that, (in the state which it implies), feudal princes may be set up, and the hosts put in motion, with advantage.
sections.What it asks: Enthusiasm. Gate 16 in the Throat Center represents skills expressed with enthusiasm—the capacity to articulate your talents, to express your depth of knowledge or ability with genuine excitement that's contagious rather than performative. The classical hexagram shows thunder emerging from earth, suggesting that true enthusiasm comes from depth rather than surface. In Human Design's reading, this becomes whether you have consistent energy for expressing your skills enthusiastically. If this gate is defined in your Throat, there's regular capacity for sharing what you know with natural excitement that engages others. You might be someone whose enthusiasm for your skills is genuine and inspiring, who can express depth accessibly. If undefined, your expression of skills is more neutral or you learn about enthusiastic expression from others. The shadow appears when enthusiasm becomes performance (trying to seem excited to impress), when skill expression becomes showing off, or when fear of appearing too enthusiastic suppresses genuine excitement about what you know. The gift is infectious enthusiasm—your genuine excitement about your skills actually helps others access enthusiasm for theirs. You can express depth without pretension and skill without superiority because your enthusiasm is real, not calculated. Practically, this gate often shows up as being told 'your passion is inspiring' or finding that when you share your skills enthusiastically, people want to learn. This is contemplative territory about the relationship between depth, skill, and genuine excitement.

sections.Text: Sui indicates that (under its conditions) there will be great progress and success. But it will be advantageous to be firm and correct. There will (then) be no error.
sections.What it asks: Following. Gate 17 in the Ajna Center represents opinions—the mental capacity to form perspectives, to organize ideas into coherent viewpoints, and to offer these as possibilities for others to consider or follow. The classical hexagram suggests that following comes naturally when there's something worth following, when opinions serve rather than dominate. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes whether you have consistent access to opinion formation. If this gate is defined in your Ajna, there's regular energy for forming mental perspectives. You might be someone who naturally has opinions about things, who can organize disparate information into coherent viewpoints, whose perspectives help others think more clearly. If undefined, your thinking is more open and questioning, sampling opinions from others without needing to form fixed views. The shadow appears when opinions harden into dogma, when you need others to follow your thinking to validate yourself, or when having opinions becomes more important than discovering truth. The gift is helpful perspective—your opinions actually serve others' thinking rather than shutting it down. You can hold views strongly while remaining genuinely curious about other perspectives. Practically, this gate often manifests as people saying 'what's your take on this?' or finding that your perspectives help groups move forward when thinking gets stuck. This is contemplative territory about the relationship between conviction and openness.

items.name: 18 · Work on what has been spoiled [Decay]

sections.Scenery: Mountain over Wind. (The trigram for) a mountain, and below it that for wind, form Kû. The superior man, in accordance with this, (addresses himself to) help the people and nourish his own virtue.
sections.Text: Kû indicates great progress and success (to him who deals properly with the condition represented by it). There will be advantage in (efforts like that of) crossing the great stream. (He should weigh well, however, the events of) three days before the turning point, and those (to be done) three days after it.
sections.What it asks: Work on the Decayed. Gate 18 in the Spleen Center represents correction—the instinctual capacity to recognize what's not working, what needs repair or improvement, and to challenge patterns that have become corrupt or dysfunctional. The classical hexagram addresses decay and the work required to address what has spoiled, suggesting that correction is not just criticism but active repair. In Human Design's reading, this becomes whether you have consistent instinctual knowing about what needs fixing. If this gate is defined in your Spleen, there's regular intuitive capacity for seeing what's wrong and feeling compelled to address it. You might be someone who naturally spots problems, who can't let dysfunction continue unchallenged, whose corrections ultimately serve health. If undefined, you're less focused on what's wrong and may need others to point out problems. The shadow appears when correction becomes constant criticism without constructive action, when perfectionism makes everything seem broken, or when you focus so much on what's wrong that you miss what's working. The gift is healing judgment—your capacity to see dysfunction actually helps systems repair themselves. You challenge not to destroy but to restore health. Practically, this gate often manifests as being the person who says what everyone's thinking but won't say, whose challenges ultimately strengthen rather than weaken systems. This is contemplative territory about the difference between destructive criticism and healing correction.

sections.Scenery: Earth over Lake. (The trigram for) the waters of a marsh and that for the earth above it form Lin. The superior man, in accordance with this, has his purposes of instruction that are inexhaustible, and nourishes and supports the people without limit.
sections.Text: Lin indicates that under the conditions supposed in it there will be great progress and success, while it will be advantageous to be firmly correct. In the eighth month there will be evil.
sections.What it asks: Approach. Gate 19 in the Root Center represents wanting—the pressure to approach basic needs, to be sensitive to what's required for survival and thriving, and to ensure that fundamental resources are available. The classical hexagram suggests approach as both movement toward what's needed and the way needs approach us as demands. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes whether you have consistent pressure around needs and resources. If this gate is defined in your Root, there's regular awareness of what's needed—not just for you but often for others or the collective. You might be someone who's keenly aware of resource issues, who can't ignore when basic needs aren't met, who feels pressure to ensure adequacy. If undefined, you're less focused on need states and may experience wanting in waves or learn about it from others. The shadow appears when sensitivity to needs becomes anxiety about scarcity, when wanting becomes grasping that never feels satisfied, or when awareness of others' needs leads to martyrdom or resentment. The gift is sensitive provision—your awareness of what's truly needed helps resources flow where they serve life. You can distinguish real needs from manufactured wants. Practically, this gate often manifests as noticing when someone needs something before they ask, organizing resource sharing, or feeling unable to rest when basic needs are unmet around you. This is contemplative territory about the relationship between need, want, and sufficiency.

sections.Scenery: Wind over Earth. (The trigram representing) the earth, and that for wind moving above it, form Kwan. The ancient kings, in accordance with this, examined the (different) regions (of the kingdom), to see the (ways of the) people, and set forth their instructions.
sections.Text: Kwân shows (how he whom it represents should be like) the worshipper who has washed his hands, but not (yet) presented his offerings;—with sincerity and an appearance of dignity (commanding reverent regard).
sections.What it asks: Contemplation. Gate 20 in the Throat Center represents the now—the capacity to be present in this moment and to express from that presence rather than from memory or anticipation. The classical hexagram emphasizes contemplation as a form of knowing through witnessing, through being truly present to what is. In Human Design's reading, this becomes whether you have consistent access to present-moment awareness that you can articulate. If this gate is defined in your Throat, there's regular capacity for expressing from nowness. You might be someone who speaks from what's actually happening rather than from scripts, whose words have immediacy and presence, who can bring people into the present moment through your expression. If undefined, your expression may be more conceptual or historical, learning about presence from others. The shadow appears when 'being present' becomes a spiritual performance, when you use nowness to avoid responsibility for past or future, or when you're so focused on this moment that you lose continuity. The gift is genuine presence—your expression comes from actually being here, which helps others arrive too. You can articulate the present moment in ways that wake people up from habitual patterns. Practically, this gate often manifests as people saying 'you really see me' or finding that your words land with unusual impact because they come from true presence. This is contemplative territory about the relationship between awareness and expression.

sections.Wound: Chapter 11 is 'Showing Up for the Conversation' — tarot, oracular practice, the therapeutic mechanism of symbolic reframing. Hexagram 20 IS contemplation — the practice of looking deeply. The I Ching's word for this hexagram, 觀 (guān), means both 'to look' and 'to show.' The tower is where you look out AND where you are seen. When you draw a tarot card or throw I Ching coins, you're not just consulting an oracle — you're BEING consulted. The hexagram reads you. The practice is mutual: you contemplate the symbol, and the symbol contemplates you. That's what Chapter 11 discovered about tarot. Hexagram 20 makes it explicit.

sections.Scenery: Fire over Thunder. (The trigrams representing) thunder and lightning form Shih Ho. The ancient kings, in accordance with this, framed their penalties with intelligence, and promulgated their laws.
sections.Text: Shih Ho indicates successful progress (in the condition of things which it supposes). It will be advantageous to use legal constraints.
sections.What it asks: Biting Through. Gate 21 in the Heart/Ego Center represents control—the willful capacity to manage resources, to maintain authority over what belongs to you, and to bite through obstacles when necessary. The classical hexagram uses the metaphor of biting through something that blocks the mouth, suggesting that force is sometimes required for breakthrough. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes whether you have consistent access to willpower and resource management. If this gate is defined in your Heart/Ego, there's regular capacity for taking control when needed. You might be someone who can manage resources effectively, who has natural authority, who can apply will to break through resistance. If undefined, your relationship to control and authority is more fluid, learning from others about effective management. The shadow appears when control becomes domination, when willpower overrides wisdom, or when you need to control everything to feel safe. The gift is right use of authority—your capacity to control serves larger purposes rather than ego gratification. You know when to take charge and when to release control. Practically, this gate often manifests as people naturally looking to you to manage resources or make executive decisions, or finding that you can break through stuck situations through clear authority. This is contemplative territory about power, control, and service.

sections.Scenery: Mountain over Fire. (The trigram representing) a mountain and that for fire under it form Pî. The superior man, in accordance with this, throws a brilliancy around his various processes of government, but does not dare (in a similar way) to decide cases of criminal litigation.
sections.Text: Pî indicates that there should be free course (in what it denotes). There will be little advantage (however) if it be allowed to advance (and take the lead).
sections.What it asks: Grace. Gate 22 in the Solar Plexus Center represents grace and openness—the emotional capacity to listen without agenda, to be receptive to others' feelings and expressions, and to respond with grace rather than reactivity. The classical hexagram uses adornment as metaphor, suggesting that true grace is not superficial decoration but the natural beauty that emerges from inner clarity. In Human Design's reading, this becomes whether you have consistent emotional openness to receive others. If this gate is defined in your Solar Plexus, there's regular capacity for emotional listening and graceful response. You might be someone who can hear difficult emotions without defending, whose openness helps others express what's really happening emotionally. If undefined, your emotional openness comes in waves or is learned situationally. The shadow appears when openness becomes doormat energy where you receive everything without boundaries, when grace becomes performance masking inner turmoil, or when you're so open to others' emotions that you lose your own. The gift is graceful receptivity—your emotional openness actually helps others find their own emotional clarity. You can listen to intense feelings without collapsing or fixing. Practically, this gate often manifests as people feeling safe to express difficult emotions around you, or finding that your graceful presence helps de-escalate emotional intensity. This is contemplative territory about emotional boundaries and genuine openness.

sections.Scenery: Mountain over Earth. (The trigrams representing) the earth, and (above it) that for a mountain, which adheres to the earth, form Po. Superiors, in accordance with this, seek to strengthen those below them, to secure the peace and stability of their own position.
sections.Text: Po indicates that (in the state which it symbolises) it will not be advantageous to make a movement in any direction whatever.
sections.What it asks: Splitting Apart. Gate 23 in the Throat Center represents assimilation—the capacity to take in complex information and split it apart into understandable pieces that can be expressed to others. The classical hexagram warns about times when things are falling apart and suggests knowing when to act versus when to wait. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes whether you have consistent capacity to break down complexity and express it clearly. If this gate is defined in your Throat, there's regular energy for assimilating and explaining. You might be someone who can take complicated concepts and make them accessible, who explains things so others understand, whose gift is translating complexity into clarity. If undefined, your expression may be more about feeling or direct experience than explanation. The shadow appears when assimilation becomes over-simplification that loses essential nuance, when you explain things to death rather than letting people discover, or when your capacity to split things apart becomes destructive analysis. The gift is clarifying complexity—your ability to break things down actually helps people engage with difficult material. You make the complex approachable without dumbing it down. Practically, this gate often manifests as being asked to explain things, writing clear documentation, or finding that your ability to articulate complexity serves groups. This is contemplative territory about the relationship between complexity and accessibility.

sections.Scenery: Earth over Thunder. (The trigram representing) the earth and that for thunder in the midst of it form Fû. The ancient kings, in accordance with this, on the day. of the (winter) solstice, shut the gates of the passes (from one state to another), so that the travelling merchants could not (then) pursue their journeys, nor the princes go on with the inspection of their states.
sections.Text: Fû indicates that there will be free course and progress (in what it denotes). (The subject of it) finds no one to distress him in his exits and entrances; friends come to him, and no error is committed. He will return and repeat his (proper) course. In seven days comes his return. There will be advantage in whatever direction movement is made.
sections.What it asks: Return. Gate 24 in the Ajna Center represents return—the mental capacity to come back to thoughts, to rationalize and re-think, to cycle through ideas until understanding clarifies. The classical hexagram emphasizes natural cycles of return, the way things come back around at their proper time. In Human Design's reading, this becomes whether you have consistent mental energy for returning to thoughts. If this gate is defined in your Ajna, there's regular capacity for mental cycling. You might be someone who thinks about things repeatedly, who returns to ideas to refine understanding, whose thinking has a spiraling quality that deepens over time. If undefined, your thinking is more linear or you move on from ideas rather than cycling back. The shadow appears when return becomes obsessive rumination, when you can't let thoughts go even when they're resolved, or when cycling back becomes avoidance of moving forward. The gift is deepening understanding—your capacity to return to thoughts actually helps you discover layers that weren't visible on first pass. You know that understanding often requires multiple returns, that the seventh day brings different insight than the first. Practically, this gate often manifests as people saying 'I've been thinking more about what you said' or finding that your best insights come when you return to questions you thought you'd finished with. This is contemplative territory about the relationship between repetition and depth.

sections.Wound: Chapter 4 is Making Amends — the AA tradition of returning to the people you've harmed. Hexagram 24 is literally called 'Return.' In Hebrew, teshuvah means the same thing: turning back. The hexagram shows one bright line appearing at the bottom of five dark ones. The amends is not dramatic. It's the first flicker. The single honest sentence after years of silence. 'I was wrong. I'm sorry. What can I do?' That's thunder within the earth — barely audible, but the whole cycle turns on it.

sections.Scenery: Heaven over Thunder. The thunder rolls all under the sky, and to (every)thing there is given (its nature), free from all insincerity. The ancient kings, in accordance with this, (made their regulations) in complete accordance with the seasons, thereby nourishing all things.
sections.Text: Wû Wang indicates great progress and success, while there will be advantage in being firm and correct. If (its subject and his action) be not correct, he will fall into errors, and it will not be advantageous for him to move in any direction.
sections.What it asks: Innocence. Gate 25 in the Heart/Ego Center represents the spirit of the self—the innocent, spontaneous expression of who you are before conditioning, before trying to be someone. The classical hexagram emphasizes acting from natural alignment rather than calculated strategy. In Human Design's reading, this becomes whether you have consistent access to innocent, unconditional love and spontaneous self-expression. If this gate is defined in your Heart/Ego, there's regular capacity for being innocently yourself, for universal love that doesn't require earning. You might be someone who radiates unconditional acceptance, whose presence reminds others of innocence. If undefined, you experience innocence in waves or learn about unconditional love from others. The shadow appears when innocence becomes naiveté that refuses to see reality, when spirit bypasses necessary development, or when unconditional love becomes inability to set boundaries. The gift is genuine innocence—not childishness but the capacity to meet life freshly without armoring, to love without agenda. You can be fully in the world while maintaining contact with unconditioned spirit. Practically, this gate often manifests as people feeling unconditionally accepted in your presence, or finding that you can see the innocent self in others even when they've lost touch with it. This is contemplative territory about the relationship between innocence and maturity.

items.name: 26 · The Taming Power of the Great

sections.Scenery: Mountain over Heaven. (The trigram representing) a mountain, and in the midst of it that (representing) heaven, form Tâ Khû. The superior man, in accordance with this, stores largely in his memory the words and deeds of former men, to subserve the accumulation of his virtue.
sections.Text: Under the conditions of Tâ Khû it will be advantageous to be firm and correct. (If its subject do not seek to) enjoy his revenues in his own family (without taking service at court), there will be good fortune. It will be advantageous for him to cross the great stream.
sections.What it asks: Taming Power of the Great. Gate 26 in the Heart/Ego Center represents the egoist—the capacity to have a strong, integrated sense of self that serves through taming great power. This isn't ego in the negative sense but self-integrity that can contain and direct substantial force. The classical hexagram emphasizes accumulating and taming power through discipline. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes whether you have consistent access to ego strength and the capacity to sell or influence. If this gate is defined in your Heart/Ego, there's regular willpower and self-integrity. You might be someone with strong ego in the positive sense, who can accumulate resources and influence, who has natural sales ability. If undefined, your relationship to ego and influence is more situational. The shadow appears when ego becomes narcissism, when taming power becomes controlling everything, or when selling becomes manipulation. The gift is integrated strength—your ego is strong enough to contain great power without being corrupted by it. You can influence and sell ethically because your integrity remains intact. Practically, this gate often manifests as natural ability to influence others, comfort with ego strength, or finding that people trust you to handle power responsibly. This is contemplative territory about ego, power, and integrity.

items.name: 27 · The Corners of the Mouth (Providing Nourishment)

sections.Scenery: Mountain over Thunder. (The trigram representing) a mountain and under it that for thunder form Î. The superior man, in accordance with this, (enjoins) watchfulness over our words, and the temperate regulation of our eating and drinking.
sections.Text: Î indicates that with firm correctness there will be good fortune (in what is denoted by it). We must look at what we are seeking to nourish, and by the exercise of our thoughts seek for the proper aliment.
sections.What it asks: Nourishment. Gate 27 in the Sacral Center represents caring and nourishment—the life force energy for taking care of others, for providing what's needed, for nourishing both literally and metaphorically. The classical hexagram emphasizes both physical nourishment and being careful about what we take in and express. In Human Design's reading, this becomes whether you have consistent sacral energy for caregiving. If this gate is defined in your Sacral, there's regular life force available for caring. You might be someone who naturally takes care of others, who has energy for nourishing, who feels responsible for others' wellbeing. If undefined, you experience caring in waves or learn about nurturing from others. The shadow appears when caring becomes caretaking that depletes you, when responsibility becomes martyrdom, or when you only feel valuable when nourishing others. The gift is sustainable caring—your capacity to nourish actually regenerates you because it comes from genuine life force rather than obligation. You know the difference between healthy caregiving and codependence. Practically, this gate often manifests as people naturally turning to you for care, finding that you have energy for nurturing that doesn't deplete, or discovering that caring for others is how you express your life force. This is contemplative territory about the relationship between caring and depletion.

sections.Text: Tâ Kwo suggests to us a beam that is weak. There will be advantage in moving (under its conditions) in any direction whatever; there will be success.
sections.What it asks: Preponderance of the Great. Gate 28 in the Spleen Center represents risk—the instinctual knowing about when struggle is worthwhile, when taking risks serves purpose, when the game is worth playing despite difficulty. The classical hexagram warns of excess weight, the ridgepole bending, suggesting that sometimes carrying too much requires action. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes whether you have consistent instinctual knowing about meaningful risk. If this gate is defined in your Spleen, there's regular intuitive capacity for assessing when struggle serves purpose. You might be someone who knows instinctually which battles to fight, who can engage with risk when it matters, who understands that some purposes require accepting challenge. If undefined, you experience risk assessment in the moment or learn from others about purposeful struggle. The shadow appears when you seek struggle for its own sake, when every challenge seems worth taking, or when you avoid all risk and miss meaningful purpose. The gift is purposeful risk—you know which struggles serve life and which just exhaust. You can engage with challenge when it matters without becoming addicted to difficulty. Practically, this gate often manifests as people trusting your judgment about which risks are worthwhile, or finding that you're willing to struggle for what truly matters while letting go of meaningless conflict. This is contemplative territory about purpose and risk.

sections.Scenery: Water over Water. (The representation of) water flowing on continuously forms the repeated Khan. The superior man, in accordance with this, maintains constantly the virtue (of his heart) and (the integrity of) his conduct, and practises the business of instruction.
sections.Text: Khan, here repeated, shows the possession of sincerity, through which the mind is penetrating. Action (in accordance with this) will be of high value.
sections.What it asks: The Abysmal Water. Gate 29 in the Sacral Center represents commitment—the sacral energy to say yes fully, to commit life force to what you engage with, to stay with things even when they're difficult. The classical hexagram shows water doubled, emphasizing persistence through danger. In Human Design's reading, this becomes whether you have consistent sacral power for commitment. If this gate is defined in your Sacral, there's regular life force available for sustained engagement. You might be someone who commits deeply to what you say yes to, who has staying power, whose perseverance is remarkable. If undefined, commitment comes in waves or you learn about perseverance from others. The shadow appears when commitment becomes inability to quit what's no longer serving, when you stay with things from obligation rather than genuine yes, or when perseverance becomes stubbornness. The gift is full engagement—when you commit, it's with your whole life force, which paradoxically means you only commit to what deserves that energy. You know the difference between wise perseverance and pointless persistence. Practically, this gate often manifests as remarkable follow-through on what you commit to, or finding that you need to be very selective about what you say yes to because once you're in, you're really in. This is contemplative territory about commitment and discernment.

sections.Wound: Chapter 2 asks: what is the cry beneath the fight? Hexagram 29 IS that cry. The Abysmal is not about falling into danger — it's about the danger you were already in. The attachment wound. The pit you've been circling since childhood. Bowlby watched children separate from their mothers and saw protest, despair, detachment. That's Water in the Pit: you cry (protest), you go quiet (despair), you stop needing (detachment). The I Ching says: 'If you are sincere, you have success in your heart, and whatever you do succeeds.' Sincerity here means naming the pit. Not climbing out. Naming it.

sections.Scenery: Fire over Fire. (The trigram for) brightness, repeated, forms Lî. The great man, in accordance with this, cultivates more and more his brilliant (virtue), and diffuses its brightness over the four quarters (of the land).
sections.Text: Lî indicates that, (in regard to what it denotes), it will be advantageous to be firm and correct, and that thus there will be free course and success. Let (its subject) also nourish (a docility like that of) the cow, and there will be good fortune.
sections.What it asks: The Clinging Fire. Gate 30 in the Solar Plexus Center represents recognition of feelings—the emotional capacity to acknowledge desire, to recognize what you truly feel beyond what you think you should feel, to allow feelings their full intensity. The classical hexagram shows fire doubled, suggesting both illumination and the consuming nature of intensity. In Human Design's reading, this becomes whether you have consistent access to emotional intensity and desire. If this gate is defined in your Solar Plexus, there's regular experience of strong feelings. You might be someone who feels things intensely, who recognizes and honors desire, whose emotional life is rich and sometimes overwhelming. If undefined, you experience emotional intensity in waves or sample it from others. The shadow appears when intensity becomes addiction to drama, when you cling to feelings beyond their natural duration, or when recognizing desire means you must act on every feeling. The gift is emotional clarity—your capacity to recognize and honor feelings without being consumed by them. You know that feelings are information, not commands. Practically, this gate often manifests as helping others recognize their true feelings, or finding that your emotional intensity, when honored rather than suppressed, actually illuminates what matters. This is contemplative territory about the relationship between feelings and fate.

sections.Text: Hsien indicates that, (on the fulfilment of the conditions implied in it), there will be free course and success. Its advantageousness will depend on the being firm and correct, (as) in marrying a young lady. There will be good fortune.
sections.What it asks: Influence. The gift is democratic leadership—your influence comes from saying what serves the collective rather than what serves your ego. You lead with words that empower rather than diminish. Practically, this gate often manifests as people following your suggestions, your words shaping group direction, or finding that when you speak up, things shift. This is contemplative territory about voice, influence, and service.

sections.Wound: Chapter 7 is 'The Comfortable Bondage' — Andreotti's hospicing of modernity, the extraction economy we're all inside. Hexagram 47 names what that feels like from within: oppression that you can't even articulate, because 'when one has something to say, it is not believed.' The lake is drained. You can see the empty basin. You can point at it. No one believes you. That's the comfortable bondage — the exhaustion of living inside a system that extracts while insisting it provides. The I Ching's radical move: 'Success.' Even in oppression. Not because oppression is good, but because naming it — even when no one believes you — is its own kind of arrival.

sections.Scenery: Water over Wind. (The trigram representing) wood and above it that for water form Žing. The superior man, in accordance with this, comforts the people, and. stimulates them to mutual helpfulness.
sections.Text: (Looking at) Žing, (we think of) how (the site of) a town may be changed, while (the fashion of) its wells undergoes no change. (The water of a well) never disappears and never receives (any great) increase, and those who come and those who go can draw and enjoy the benefit. If (the drawing) have nearly been accomplished, but, before the rope has quite reached the water, the bucket is broken, this is evil.

The gift is genuine depth—your capacity to develop real expertise actually provides resources others can draw on. Like a well, your depth serves community. Practically, this gate often manifests as becoming expert in your areas of focus, feeling driven to truly understand rather than just know about, or finding that your depth helps solve complex problems.

sections.Wound: Chapter 8 is 'The First Fire' — the 50,000-year-old practice of controlled burning, and the catastrophic burning that happens when you forget how. Hexagram 49 is Fire under Lake: the revolution that happens when elements that should be separate meet. Aboriginal fire-tending is revolution in the I Ching's sense — not violent overthrow but intentional transformation. Molting. The snake doesn't fight its old skin. It grows a new one and the old one falls away. The I Ching says revolution succeeds 'on your own day' — when the time is right. Not forced. Not scheduled. Felt. The fire-tenders read the land. The land tells them when to burn. Revolution as listening.

sections.What it asks: The Cauldron. Gate 50 in the Spleen Center represents values—the instinctual knowing about what truly matters, about right responsibility and care, about nourishing what deserves nourishment. The classical hexagram uses the cauldron as metaphor for containing and transforming. In Human Design's reading, this becomes whether you have consistent instinctual knowing about values. If this gate is defined in your Spleen, there's regular intuitive clarity about what has value, about proper responsibility, about what deserves care. You might be someone with strong sense of values, who knows instinctually what's worth protecting, whose care serves life. If undefined, values are more situational or learned intellectually. The shadow appears when values become dogma you impose on others, when responsibility becomes controlling what everyone should value, or when care becomes codependence. The gift is clear values—your instinctual knowing about what matters actually helps communities clarify their own values. You can hold values strongly while respecting others' different values. Practically, this gate often manifests as being trusted as caretaker, clarity about what deserves resources, or finding that your values guide important decisions.

sections.Wound: Chapter 6 asks: What Survives the Turning? The caldron is the answer. Not the raw materials — they change. Not the fire — it burns out and is relit. The caldron itself: the PRACTICE of transformation. The vessel. Every culture that survived did so not because its content was superior but because it had a caldron — a way of cooking new experience into something nourishing. The commons. The village fire. The grandmother's recipe. The I Ching itself is a caldron: 3,000 years of raw experience cooked into 64 hexagrams. What survives the turning is the turning itself.

sections.Scenery: Thunder over Thunder. (The trigram representing) thunder, being repeated, forms Kăn. The superior man, in accordance with this, is fearful and apprehensive, cultivates (his virtue), and examines (his faults).
sections.Text: Kăn gives the intimation of ease and development. When (the time of) movement (which it indicates) comes, (the subject of the hexagram) will be found looking out with apprehension, and yet smiling and talking cheerfully. When the movement (like a crash of thunder) terrifies all within a hundred lî, he will be (like the sincere worshipper) who is not (startled into) letting go his ladle and (cup of) sacrificial spirits.
sections.What it asks: The Arousing. Gate 51 in the Heart/Ego Center represents shock—the ego's capacity to respond to the unexpected, to compete when aroused, to take initiative when life shocks you into action. The classical hexagram shows thunder doubled, emphasizing arousal and awakening. In Human Design's reading, this becomes whether you have consistent ego energy for responding to shock. If this gate is defined in your Heart/Ego, there's regular capacity for handling shock, for competitive response when provoked, for willpower that emerges through challenge. You might be someone who responds well under pressure, whose ego strengthens through shock, who has competitive spirit. If undefined, shock affects you more deeply or you learn about competitive response from others. The shadow appears when you seek shock to feel alive, when competition becomes your only mode, or when ego needs constant arousal to feel worthy. The gift is resilient response—your capacity to handle shock actually helps you and others move through unexpected challenges. You can compete without destroying. Practically, this gate often manifests as performing well under pressure, capacity to respond quickly to shocks, or finding that competition brings out your best.

sections.Scenery: Mountain over Mountain. (Two trigrams representing) a mountain, one over the other, form Kăn. The superior man, in accordance with this, does not go in his thoughts beyond the (duties of the) position in which he is.
sections.Text: When one's resting is like that of the back, and he loses all consciousness of self; when he walks in his courtyard, and does not see any (of the persons) in it,—there will be no error.
sections.What it asks: Keeping Still. Gate 52 in the Root Center represents stillness—the pressure to be still, to concentrate, to meditate, to stop activity and just be. The classical hexagram shows mountain doubled, emphasizing stillness and stability. In Human Design's reading, this becomes whether you have consistent pressure toward stillness and concentration. If this gate is defined in your Root, there's regular pressure to be still, to concentrate deeply, to meditate or practice focused inaction. You might be someone who needs regular stillness to function, whose depth comes from concentrated attention, who feels pressure to stop and be present. If undefined, stillness comes naturally or you're more comfortable with activity. The shadow appears when stillness becomes paralysis, when concentration becomes fixation, or when pressure to be still makes you unable to act when action is needed. The gift is concentrated presence—your capacity for stillness actually creates the ground for wise action. You know that doing comes from being. Practically, this gate often manifests as needing meditation or stillness practice, capacity for deep concentration, or finding that your stillness helps others settle.

sections.Text: Kien suggests to us the marriage of a young lady, and the good fortune (attending it). There will be advantage in being firm and correct.
sections.What it asks: Development. Gate 53 in the Root Center represents beginnings—the pressure to start things, to begin cycles, to initiate development through gradual, orderly progress. The classical hexagram emphasizes gradual development like a tree growing on a mountain. In Human Design's reading, this becomes whether you have consistent pressure to begin and develop. You might be someone who feels compelled to start cycles, whose pressure to begin helps things evolve, who initiates gradual development. If undefined, beginning pressure comes situationally or you're more comfortable continuing what others start. The shadow appears when you start things compulsively without completing them, when beginning pressure scatters your energy, or when you can't rest in what's already begun. The gift is purposeful initiation—your pressure to begin actually serves necessary evolution. You know which beginnings deserve energy. Practically, this gate often manifests as naturally starting new things, feeling restless when nothing new is beginning, or finding that your initiation helps groups evolve.

sections.Wound: Chapter 9 is 'A Vocation, Not a Prophecy' — Parker Palmer's listening for what your life wants to be. Hexagram 53 is the I Ching's most patient hexagram. The wild goose doesn't rush to the shore. It lands on a rock, then a cliff, then a hill, then a tree, then a summit, then high clouds. Each stage is complete in itself AND part of a journey. That's vocation: not a destination but a gradual approach. Palmer says 'before you tell your life what you intend to do with it, listen for what it intends to do with you.' The wild goose listens to the wind. The tree listens to the mountain. Vocation is the gradual progress of becoming what you already are.

sections.Scenery: Thunder over Lake. (The trigram representing the waters of) a marsh and over it that for thunder form Kwei Mei. The superior man, in accordance with this, having regard to the far-distant end, knows the mischief (that may be done at the beginning).
sections.Text: Kwei Mei indicates that (under the conditions which it denotes) action will be evil, and in no wise advantageous.
sections.What it asks: The Marrying Maiden. Gate 54 in the Root Center represents ambition—the pressure to transform your position, to marry into something better, to drive toward ascension through relationship or connection. The classical hexagram warns about improper ambition and relationships. In Human Design's reading, this becomes whether you have consistent pressure around ambition and transformation. If this gate is defined in your Root, there's regular pressure to improve your position, to transform through connection, to be ambitious about where you're going. You might be someone driven to ascend, whose ambition seeks right relationships, who feels pressure to transform circumstances. If undefined, ambition comes in waves or you're more content with your current position. The shadow appears when ambition becomes using others for advancement, when you'll do anything to transform your position, or when drive to ascend makes you unable to appreciate where you are. The gift is right ambition—your drive to transform actually helps you and others rise together. You know that true ascension serves collective good. Practically, this gate often manifests as strategic about relationships and connections, drive to improve circumstances, or finding that ambition motivates sustained effort.

sections.Scenery: Thunder over Fire. (The trigrams representing) thunder and lightning combine to form Făng. The superior man, in accordance with this, decides cases of litigation, and apportions punishments with exactness.
sections.Text: Făng intimates progress and development. When a king has reached the point (which the name denotes) there is no occasion to be anxious (through fear of a change). Let him be as the sun at noon.
sections.What it asks: Abundance. sections.Text: Lü intimates that (in the condition which it denotes) there may be some little attainment and progress. If the stranger or traveller be firm and correct as he ought to be, there will be good fortune.

sections.What it asks: The Gentle. sections.Wound: Chapter 3 is 'Hold Me Tight' — Sue Johnson's EFT, the vulnerability request that repairs by reaching rather than defending. Hexagram 58 is the I Ching's version: two lakes, connected underground, each feeding the other. Joy in the I Ching is not happiness — it's resonance. The kind that happens when you say 'I need you' and the other person doesn't flinch. The connected lake. The image says: 'Thus the superior person joins with friends for discussion and practice.' Repair is never solo. Two lakes, or nothing.

sections.Text: Hwân intimates that (under its conditions) there will be progress and success. The king goes to his ancestral temple; and it will be advantageous to cross the great stream. It will be advantageous to be firm and correct.
sections.What it asks: Dispersion. The gift is generative intimacy—your capacity to open actually creates genuine connection. You know that true intimacy requires dispersion of false walls while maintaining healthy boundaries. Practically, this gate often manifests as capacity for deep intimacy, comfort with vulnerability, or finding that your openness helps others open.

sections.Text: Hsiâo Kwo indicates that (in the circumstances which it implies) there will be progress and attainment. But it will be advantageous to be firm and correct. The shadow appears when doubt becomes cynicism that believes nothing, when questioning prevents ever reaching conclusions, or when skepticism isolates you from connection.
