sections.Judgment: In (what is denoted by) Sun, if there be sincerity (in him who employs it), there will be great good fortune:—freedom from error; firmness and correctness that can be maintained; and advantage in every movement that shall be made. In what shall this (sincerity in the exercise of Sun) be employed? (Even) in sacrifice two baskets of grain, (though there be nothing else), may be presented.
sections.Line 1: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject suspending his own affairs, and hurrying away (to help the subject of the fourth line). He will commit no error, but let him consider how far he should contribute of what is his (for the other).
sections.Line 2: The second NINE, undivided, shows that it will be advantageous for its subject to maintain a firm correctness, and that action on his part will be evil. He can give increase (to his correlate) without taking from himself.
sections.Line 3: The third SIX, divided, shows how of three men walking together, the number is diminished by one; and how one, walking, finds his friend.
sections.Line 4: The fourth SIX, divided, shows its subject diminishing the ailment under which he labours by making (the subject of the first line) hasten (to his help), and make him glad. There will be no error.
sections.Line 5: The fifth SIX, divided, shows parties adding to (the stores of) its subject ten pairs of tortoise shells, and accepting no refusal. There will be great good fortune.
sections.Line 6: The topmost NINE, undivided, shows its subject giving increase to others without taking from himself. There will be no error. With firm correctness there will be good fortune. There will be advantage in every movement that shall be made. He will find ministers more than can be counted by their clans.

metadata._source: James Legge (tr.), The Yî King, Sacred Books of the East vol. XVI (Oxford, 1882; 2nd ed. 1899), Text — public domain. Wording cross-verified across three independent digitizations (sacred-texts.com transcription + two independently maintained datasets).

sections.Judgment: Yî indicates that (in the state which it denotes) there will be advantage in every movement which shall be undertaken, that it will be advantageous (even) to cross the great stream.
sections.Line 1: The first NINE, undivided, shows that it will be advantageous for its subject in his position to make a great movement. If it be greatly fortunate, no blame will be imputed to him.
sections.Line 2: The second SIX, divided, shows parties adding to the stores of its subject ten pairs of tortoise shells whose oracles cannot be opposed. Let him persevere in being firm and correct, and there will be good fortune. Let the king, (having the virtues thus distinguished), employ them in presenting his offerings to God, and there will be good fortune.
sections.Line 3: The third SIX, divided, shows increase given to its subject by means of what is evil, so that he shall (be led to good), and be without blame. Let him be sincere and pursue the path of the Mean, (so shall he secure the recognition of the ruler, like) an officer who announces himself to his prince by the symbol of his rank.
sections.Line 4: The fourth SIX, divided, shows its subject pursuing the due course. His advice to his prince is followed. He can with advantage be relied on in such a movement as that of removing the capital.
sections.Line 5: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject with sincere heart seeking to benefit (all below). There need be no question about it; the result will be great good fortune. (All below) will with sincere heart acknowledge his goodness.
sections.Line 6: In the sixth NINE, undivided, we see one to whose increase none will contribute, while many will seek to assail him. He observes no regular rule in the ordering of his heart. There will be evil.

metadata._source: James Legge (tr.), The Yî King, Sacred Books of the East vol. XVI (Oxford, 1882; 2nd ed. 1899), Text — public domain. Wording cross-verified across three independent digitizations (sacred-texts.com transcription + two independently maintained datasets).

sections.Judgment: Kwâi requires (in him who would fulfil its meaning) the exhibition (of the culprit's guilt) in the royal court, and a sincere and earnest appeal (for sympathy and support), with a consciousness of the peril (involved in cutting off the criminal). He should (also) make announcement in his own city, and show that it will not be well to have recourse at once to arms. (In this way) there will be advantage in whatever he shall go forward to.
sections.Line 1: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject in (the pride of) strength advancing with his toes. He goes forward, but will not succeed. There will be ground for blame.
sections.Line 2: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject full of apprehension and appealing (for sympathy and help). Late at night hostile measures may be (taken against him), but he need not be anxious about them.
sections.Line 3: The third NINE, undivided, shows its subject (about to advance) with strong (and determined) looks. There will be evil. (But) the superior man, bent on cutting off (the criminal), will walk alone and encounter the rain, (till he be hated by his proper associates) as if he were contaminated (by the others). (In the end) there will be no blame against him.
sections.Line 4: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows one from whose buttocks the skin has been stripped, and who walks slowly and with difficulty. (If he could act) like a sheep led (after its companions), occasion for repentance would disappear. But though he hear these words, he will not believe them.
sections.Line 5: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows (the small men like) a bed of purslain, which ought to be uprooted with the utmost determination. (The subject of the line having such determination), his action, in harmony with his central position, will lead to no error or blame.
sections.Line 6: The sixth SIX, divided, shows its subject without any (helpers) on whom to call. His end will be evil.

metadata._source: James Legge (tr.), The Yî King, Sacred Books of the East vol. XVI (Oxford, 1882; 2nd ed. 1899), Text — public domain. Wording cross-verified across three independent digitizations (sacred-texts.com transcription + two independently maintained datasets).

sections.Judgment: Kâu shows a female who is bold and strong. It will not be good to marry (such) a female.
sections.Line 1: The first SIX, divided, shows how its subject should be kept (like a carriage) tied and fastened to a metal drag, in which case with firm correctness there will be good fortune. (But) if he move in any direction, evil will appear. He will be (like) a lean pig, which is sure to keep jumping about.
sections.Line 2: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject with a wallet of fish. There will be no error. But it will not be well to let (the subject of the first line) go forward to the guests.
sections.Line 3: The third NINE, undivided, shows one from whose buttocks the skin has been stripped so that he walks with difficulty. The position is perilous, but there will be no great error.
sections.Line 4: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows its subject with his wallet, but no fish in it. This will give rise to evil.
sections.Line 5: The fifth NINE, undivided, (shows its subject as) a medlar tree overspreading the gourd (beneath it). If he keep his brilliant qualities concealed, (a good issue) will descend (as) from Heaven.
sections.Line 6: The sixth NINE, undivided, shows its subject receiving others on his horns. There will be occasion for regret, but there will be no error.

metadata._source: James Legge (tr.), The Yî King, Sacred Books of the East vol. XVI (Oxford, 1882; 2nd ed. 1899), Text — public domain. Wording cross-verified across three independent digitizations (sacred-texts.com transcription + two independently maintained datasets).

sections.Judgment: In (the state denoted by) Žhui, the king will repair to his ancestral temple. It will be advantageous (also) to meet with the great man; and then there will be progress and success, though the advantage must come through firm correctness. The use of great victims will conduce to good fortune; and in whatever direction movement is made, it will be advantageous.
sections.Line 1: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject with a sincere desire (for union), but unable to carry it out, so that disorder is brought into the sphere of his union. If he cry out (for help to his proper correlate), all at once (his tears) will give place to smiles. He need not mind (the temporary difficulty); as he goes forward, there will be no error.
sections.Line 2: The second SIX, divided, shows its subject led forward (by his correlate). There will be good fortune, and freedom from error. There is entire sincerity, and in that case (even the small offerings of) the vernal sacrifice are acceptable.
sections.Line 3: The third SIX, divided, shows its subject striving after union and seeming to sigh, yet nowhere finding any advantage. If he go forward, he will not err, though there may be some small cause for regret.
sections.Line 4: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows its subject in such a state that, if he be greatly fortunate, he will receive no blame.
sections.Line 5: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows the union (of all) under its subject in the place of dignity. There will be no error. If any do not have confidence in him, let him see to it that (his virtue) be great, long-continued, and firmly correct, and all occasion for repentance will disappear.
sections.Line 6: The topmost SIX, divided, shows its subject sighing and weeping; but there will be no error.

metadata._source: James Legge (tr.), The Yî King, Sacred Books of the East vol. XVI (Oxford, 1882; 2nd ed. 1899), Text — public domain. Wording cross-verified across three independent digitizations (sacred-texts.com transcription + two independently maintained datasets).

sections.Judgment: Shăng indicates that (under its conditions) there will be great progress and success. Seeking by (the qualities implied in it) to meet with the great man, its subject need have no anxiety. Advance to the south will be fortunate.
sections.Line 1: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject advancing upwards with the welcome (of those above him). There will be great good fortune.
sections.Line 2: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject with that sincerity which will make even the (small) offerings of the vernal sacrifice acceptable. There will be no error.
sections.Line 3: The third NINE, undivided, shows its subject ascending upwards (as into) an empty city.
sections.Line 4: The fourth SIX, divided, shows its subject employed by the king to present his offerings on mount Khî. There will be good fortune; there will be no mistake.
sections.Line 5: The fifth six, divided, shows its subject firmly correct, and therefore enjoying good fortune. He ascends the stairs (with all due ceremony).
sections.Line 6: The sixth six, divided, shows its subject advancing upwards blindly. Advantage will be found in a ceaseless maintenance of firm correctness.

metadata._source: James Legge (tr.), The Yî King, Sacred Books of the East vol. XVI (Oxford, 1882; 2nd ed. 1899), Text — public domain. Wording cross-verified across three independent digitizations (sacred-texts.com transcription + two independently maintained datasets).

sections.Judgment: In (the condition denoted by) Khwăn there may (yet be) progress and success. For the firm and correct, the (really) great man, there will be good fortune. He will fall into no error. If he make speeches, his words cannot be made good.
sections.Line 1: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject with bare buttocks straitened under the stump of a tree. He enters a dark valley, and for three years has no prospect (of deliverance).
sections.Line 2: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject straitened amidst his wine and viands. There come to him anon the red knee-covers (of the ruler). It will be well for him (to maintain his sincerity as) in sacrificing. Active operations (on his part) will lead to evil, but he will be free from blame.
sections.Line 3: The third SIX, divided, shows its subject straitened before a (frowning) rock. He lays hold of thorns. He enters his palace, and does not see his wife. There will be evil.
sections.Line 4: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows its subject proceeding very slowly (to help the subject of the first line), who is straitened by the carriage adorned with metal in front of him. There will be occasion for regret, but the end will be good.
sections.Line 5: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject with his nose and feet cut off. He is straitened by (his ministers in their) scarlet aprons. He is leisurely in his movements, however, and is satisfied. It will be well for him to be (as sincere) as in sacrificing (to spiritual beings).
sections.Line 6: The sixth SIX, divided, shows its subject straitened, as if bound with creepers; or in a high and dangerous position, and saying (to himself), 'If I move, I shall repent it.' If he do repent of former errors, there will be good fortune in his going forward.

metadata._source: James Legge (tr.), The Yî King, Sacred Books of the East vol. XVI (Oxford, 1882; 2nd ed. 1899), Text — public domain. Wording cross-verified across three independent digitizations (sacred-texts.com transcription + two independently maintained datasets).

sections.Judgment: (Looking at) Žing, (we think of) how (the site of) a town may be changed, while (the fashion of) its wells undergoes no change. (The water of a well) never disappears and never receives (any great) increase, and those who come and those who go can draw and enjoy the benefit. If (the drawing) have nearly been accomplished, but, before the rope has quite reached the water, the bucket is broken, this is evil.
sections.Line 1: The first SIX, divided, shows a well so muddy that men will not drink of it; or an old well to which neither birds (nor other creatures) resort.
sections.Line 2: The second NINE, undivided, shows a well from which by a hole the water escapes and flows away to the shrimps (and such small creatures among the grass), or one the water of which leaks away from a broken basket.
sections.Line 3: The third NINE, undivided, shows a well, which has been cleared out, but is not used. Our hearts are sorry for this, for the water might be drawn out and used. If the king were (only) intelligent, both he and we might receive the benefit of it.
sections.Line 4: The fourth SIX, divided, shows a well, the lining of which is well laid. There will be no error.
sections.Line 5: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows a clear, limpid well, (the waters from) whose cold spring are (freely) drunk.
sections.Line 6: The topmost SIX, divided, shows (the water from) the well brought to the top, which is not allowed to be covered. This suggests the idea of sincerity. There will be great good fortune.

metadata._source: James Legge (tr.), The Yî King, Sacred Books of the East vol. XVI (Oxford, 1882; 2nd ed. 1899), Text — public domain. Wording cross-verified across three independent digitizations (sacred-texts.com transcription + two independently maintained datasets).

sections.Judgment: (What takes place as indicated by) Ko is believed in only after it has been accomplished. There will be great progress and success. Advantage will come from being firm and correct. (In that case) occasion for repentance will disappear.
sections.Line 1: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject (as if he were) bound with the skin of a yellow ox.
sections.Line 2: The second SIX, divided, shows its subject making his changes after some time has passed. Action taken will be fortunate. There will be no error.
sections.Line 3: The third NINE, undivided, shows that action taken by its subject will be evil. Though he be firm and correct, his position is perilous. If the change (he contemplates) have been three times fully discussed, he will be believed in.
sections.Line 4: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows occasion for repentance disappearing (from its subject). Let him be believed in; and though he change (existing) ordinances, there will be good fortune.
sections.Line 5: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows the great man (producing his changes) as the tiger (does when he) changes (his stripes). Before he divines (and proceeds to action), faith has been reposed in him.
sections.Line 6: The sixth SIX, divided, shows the superior man producing his changes as the leopard (does when he) changes (his spots), while small men change their faces (and show their obedience). To go forward (now) would lead to evil, but there will be good fortune in abiding firm and correct.

metadata._source: James Legge (tr.), The Yî King, Sacred Books of the East vol. XVI (Oxford, 1882; 2nd ed. 1899), Text — public domain. Wording cross-verified across three independent digitizations (sacred-texts.com transcription + two independently maintained datasets).

sections.Judgment: Ting gives the intimation of great progress and success.
sections.Line 1: The first SIX, divided, shows the caldron overthrown and its feet turned up. (But) there will be advantage in its getting rid of what was bad in it. (Or it shows us) the concubine (whose position is improved) by means of her son. There will be no error.
sections.Line 2: The second NINE, undivided, shows the caldron with the things (to be cooked) in it. (If its subject can say), 'My enemy dislikes me, but he cannot approach me,' there will be good fortune.
sections.Line 3: The third NINE, undivided, shows the caldron with (the places of) its ears changed. The progress (of its subject) is (thus) stopped. The fat flesh of the pheasant (which is in the caldron) will not be eaten. But the (genial) rain will come, and the grounds for repentance will disappear. There will be good fortune in the end.
sections.Line 4: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows the caldron with its feet broken; and its contents, designed for the ruler's use, overturned and spilt. Its Subject will be made to blush for shame. There will be evil.
sections.Line 5: The fifth SIX, divided, shows the caldron with yellow ears and rings of metal in them. There will be advantage through being firm and correct.
sections.Line 6: The sixth NINE, undivided, shows the caldron with rings of jade. There will be great good fortune, and all action taken will be in every way advantageous.

metadata._source: James Legge (tr.), The Yî King, Sacred Books of the East vol. XVI (Oxford, 1882; 2nd ed. 1899), Text — public domain. Wording cross-verified across three independent digitizations (sacred-texts.com transcription + two independently maintained datasets).

sections.Judgment: Kăn gives the intimation of ease and development. When (the time of) movement (which it indicates) comes, (the subject of the hexagram) will be found looking out with apprehension, and yet smiling and talking cheerfully. When the movement (like a crash of thunder) terrifies all within a hundred lî, he will be (like the sincere worshipper) who is not (startled into) letting go his ladle and (cup of) sacrificial spirits.
sections.Line 1: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject, when the movement approaches, looking out and around with apprehension, and afterwards smiling and talking cheerfully. There will be good fortune.
sections.Line 2: The second SIX, divided, shows its subject, when the movement approaches, in a position of peril. He judges it better to let go the articles (in his possession), and to ascend a very lofty height. There is no occasion for him to pursue after (the things he has let go); in seven days he will find them.
sections.Line 3: The third SIX, divided, shows its subject distraught amid the startling movements going on. If those movements excite him to (right) action, there will be no mistake.
sections.Line 4: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows its subject, amid the startling movements, supinely sinking (deeper) in the mud.
sections.Line 5: The fifth SIX, divided, shows its subject going and coming amidst the startling movements (of the time), and always in peril; but perhaps he will not incur loss, and find business (which he can accomplish).
sections.Line 6: The topmost SIX, divided, shows its subject, amidst the startling movements (of the time), in breathless dismay and looking round him with trembling apprehension. If he take action, there will be evil. If, while the startling movements have not reached his own person and his neighbourhood, (he were to take precautions), there would be no error, though his relatives might (still) speak against him.

sections.Judgment: When one's resting is like that of the back, and he loses all consciousness of self; when he walks in his courtyard, and does not see any (of the persons) in it,—there will be no error.
sections.Line 1: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject keeping his toes at rest. There will be no error; but it will be advantageous for him to be persistently firm and correct.
sections.Line 2: The second SIX, divided, shows its subject keeping the calves of his legs at rest. He cannot help (the subject of the line above) whom he follows, and is dissatisfied in his mind.
sections.Line 3: The third NINE, undivided, shows its subject keeping his loins at rest, and separating the ribs (from the body below). The situation is perilous, and the heart glows with suppressed excitement.
sections.Line 4: The fourth SIX, divided, shows its subject keeping his trunk at rest. There will be no error.
sections.Line 5: The fifth SIX, divided, shows its subject keeping his jawbones at rest, so that his words are (all) orderly. Occasion for repentance will disappear.
sections.Line 6: The sixth NINE, undivided, shows its subject devotedly maintaining his restfulness. There will be good fortune.

metadata._source: James Legge (tr.), The Yî King, Sacred Books of the East vol. XVI (Oxford, 1882; 2nd ed. 1899), Text — public domain. Wording cross-verified across three independent digitizations (sacred-texts.com transcription + two independently maintained datasets).

sections.Judgment: Kien suggests to us the marriage of a young lady, and the good fortune (attending it). There will be advantage in being firm and correct.
sections.Line 1: The first SIX, divided, shows the wild geese gradually approaching the shore. A young officer (in similar circumstances) will be in a position of danger, and be spoken against; but there will be no error.
sections.Line 2: The second SIX, divided, shows the geese gradually approaching the large rocks, where they eat and drink joyfully and at ease. There will be good fortune.
sections.Line 3: The third NINE, undivided, shows them gradually advanced to the dry plains. (It suggests also the idea of) a husband who goes on an expedition from which he does not return, and of a wife who is pregnant, but will not nourish her child. There will be evil. (The case symbolised) might be advantageous in resisting plunderers.
sections.Line 4: The fourth SIX, divided, shows the geese gradually advanced to the trees. They may light on the flat branches. There will be no error.
sections.Line 5: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows the geese gradually advanced to the high mound. (It suggests the idea of) a wife who for three years does not become pregnant; but in the end the natural issue cannot be prevented. There will be good fortune.
sections.Line 6: The sixth NINE, undivided, shows the geese gradually advanced to the large heights (beyond). Their feathers can be used as ornaments. There will be good fortune.

metadata._source: James Legge (tr.), The Yî King, Sacred Books of the East vol. XVI (Oxford, 1882; 2nd ed. 1899), Text — public domain. Wording cross-verified across three independent digitizations (sacred-texts.com transcription + two independently maintained datasets).

sections.Judgment: Kwei Mei indicates that (under the conditions which it denotes) action will be evil, and in no wise advantageous.
sections.Line 1: The first NINE, undivided, shows the younger sister married off in a position ancillary to the real wife. (It suggests the idea of) a person lame on one leg who yet manages to tramp along. Going forward will be fortunate.
sections.Line 2: The second NINE, undivided, shows her blind of one eye, and yet able to see. There will be advantage in her maintaining the firm correctness of a solitary widow.
sections.Line 3: The third SIX, divided, shows the younger sister who was to be married off in a mean position. She returns and accepts an ancillary position.
sections.Line 4: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows the younger sister who is to be married off protracting the time. She may be late in being married, but the time will come.
sections.Line 5: The fifth SIX, divided, reminds us of the marrying of the younger sister of (king) Tî-yî, when the sleeves of her the princess were not equal to those of the (still) younger sister who accompanied her in an inferior capacity. (The case suggests the thought of) the moon almost full. There will be good fortune.
sections.Line 6: The sixth SIX, divided, shows the young lady bearing the basket, but without anything in it, and the gentleman slaughtering the sheep, but without blood flowing from it. There will be no advantage in any way.

metadata._source: James Legge (tr.), The Yî King, Sacred Books of the East vol. XVI (Oxford, 1882; 2nd ed. 1899), Text — public domain. Wording cross-verified across three independent digitizations (sacred-texts.com transcription + two independently maintained datasets).

sections.Judgment: Făng intimates progress and development. When a king has reached the point (which the name denotes) there is no occasion to be anxious (through fear of a change). Let him be as the sun at noon.
sections.Line 1: The first NINE, undivided, shows its subject meeting with his mate. Though they are both of the same character, there will be no error. Advance will call forth approval.
sections.Line 2: The second SIX, divided, shows its subject surrounded by screens so large and thick that at midday he can see from them the constellation of the Bushel. If he go (and try to enlighten his ruler who is thus emblemed), he will make himself to be viewed with suspicion and dislike. Let him cherish his feeling of sincere devotion that he may thereby move (his ruler's mind), and there will be good fortune.
sections.Line 3: The third NINE, undivided, shows its subject with an (additional) screen of a large and thick banner, through which at midday he can see (the small) Mei star. (In the darkness) he breaks his right arm; but there will be no error.
sections.Line 4: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows its subject in a tent so large and thick that at midday he can see from it the constellation of the Bushel. But he meets with the subject of the (first) line, undivided like himself. There will be good fortune.
sections.Line 5: The fifth SIX, divided, shows its subject bringing around him the men of brilliant ability. There will be occasion for congratulation and praise. There will be good fortune.
sections.Line 6: The topmost SIX, divided, shows its subject with his house made large, but only serving as a screen to his household. When he looks at his door, it is still, and there is nobody about it. For three years no one is to be seen. There will be evil.

metadata._source: James Legge (tr.), The Yî King, Sacred Books of the East vol. XVI (Oxford, 1882; 2nd ed. 1899), Text — public domain. Wording cross-verified across three independent digitizations (sacred-texts.com transcription + two independently maintained datasets).

sections.Judgment: Lü intimates that (in the condition which it denotes) there may be some little attainment and progress. If the stranger or traveller be firm and correct as he ought to be, there will be good fortune.
sections.Line 1: The first SIX, divided, shows the stranger mean and meanly occupied. It is thus that he brings on himself (further) calamity.
sections.Line 2: The second SIX, divided, shows the stranger, occupying his lodging-house, carrying with him his means of livelihood, and provided with good and trusty servants.
sections.Line 3: The third NINE, undivided, shows the stranger, burning his lodging-house, and having lost his servants. However firm and correct he (try to) be, he will be in peril.
sections.Line 4: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows the traveller in a resting-place, having (also) the means of livelihood and the axe, (but still saying), 'I am not at ease in my mind.'
sections.Line 5: The fifth SIX, divided, shows its subject shooting a pheasant. He will lose his arrow, but in the end he will obtain praise and a (high) charge.
sections.Line 6: The sixth NINE, undivided, suggests the idea of a bird burning its nest. The stranger, (thus represented), first laughs and then cries out. He has lost his ox(-like docility) too readily and easily. There will be evil.

metadata._source: James Legge (tr.), The Yî King, Sacred Books of the East vol. XVI (Oxford, 1882; 2nd ed. 1899), Text — public domain. Wording cross-verified across three independent digitizations (sacred-texts.com transcription + two independently maintained datasets).

sections.Judgment: Sun intimates that (under the conditions which it denotes) there will be some little attainment and progress. There will be advantage in movement onward in whatever direction. It will be advantageous (also) to see the great man.
sections.Line 1: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject (now) advancing, (now) receding. It would be advantageous for him to have the firm correctness of a brave soldier.
sections.Line 2: The second NINE, undivided, shows the representative of Sun beneath a couch, and employing diviners and exorcists in a way bordering on confusion. There will be good fortune and no error.
sections.Line 3: The third NINE, undivided, shows its subject penetrating (only) by violent and repeated efforts. There will be occasion for regret.
sections.Line 4: The fourth SIX, divided, shows all occasion for repentance (in its subject) passed away. He takes game for its threefold use in his hunting.
sections.Line 5: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows that with firm correctness there will be good fortune (to its subject). All occasion for repentance will disappear, and all his movements will be advantageous. There may have been no (good) beginning, but there will be a (good) end. Three days before making any changes, (let him give notice of them); and three days after, (let him reconsider them). There will (thus) be good fortune.
sections.Line 6: The sixth NINE, undivided, shows the representative of penetration beneath a couch, and having lost the axe with which he executed his decisions. However firm and correct he may (try to) be, there will be evil.

sections.Judgment: Tui intimates that (under its conditions) there will be progress and attainment. (But) it will be advantageous to be firm and correct.

sections.Line 2: The second NINE, undivided, shows the pleasure arising from (inward) sincerity. There will be good fortune. Occasion for repentance will disappear.
sections.Line 3: The third SIX, divided, shows its subject bringing round himself whatever can give pleasure. There will be evil.
sections.Line 4: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows its subject deliberating about what to seek his pleasure in, and not at rest. He borders on what would be injurious, but there will be cause for joy.
sections.Line 5: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject trusting in one who would injure him. The situation is perilous.
sections.Line 6: The topmost SIX, divided, shows the pleasure of its subject in leading and attracting others.

sections.Judgment: Hwân intimates that (under its conditions) there will be progress and success. The king goes to his ancestral temple; and it will be advantageous to cross the great stream. It will be advantageous to be firm and correct.
sections.Line 1: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject engaged in rescuing (from the impending evil) and having (the assistance of) a strong horse. There will be good fortune.
sections.Line 2: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject, amid the dispersion, hurrying to his contrivance (for security). All occasion for repentance will disappear.
sections.Line 3: The third SIX, divided, shows its subject discarding any regard to his own person. There will be no occasion for repentance.
sections.Line 4: The fourth SIX, divided, shows its subject scattering the (different) parties (in the state); which leads to great good fortune. From the dispersion (he collects again good men standing out, a crowd) like a mound, which is what ordinary men would not have thought of.
sections.Line 5: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject amidst the dispersion issuing his great announcements as the perspiration (flows from his body). He scatters abroad (also) the accumulations in the royal granaries. There will be no error.
sections.Line 6: The topmost NINE, undivided, shows its subject disposing of (what may be called) its bloody wounds, and going and separating himself from its anxious fears. There will be no error.

sections.Judgment: Kieh intimates that (under its conditions) there will be progress and attainment. (But) if the regulations (which it prescribes) be severe and difficult, they cannot be permanent.

sections.Line 2: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject not quitting the courtyard inside his gate. There will be evil.
sections.Line 3: The third SIX, divided, shows its subject with no appearance of observing the (proper) regulations, in which case we shall see him lamenting. But there will be no one to blame (but himself).
sections.Line 4: The fourth SIX, divided, shows its subject quietly and naturally (attentive to all) regulations. There will be progress and success.
sections.Line 5: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject sweetly and acceptably enacting his regulations. There will be good fortune. The onward progress with them will afford ground for admiration.

sections.Line 2: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject (like) the crane crying out in her hidden retirement, and her young ones responding to her. (It is as if it were said), 'I have a cup of good spirits,' (and the response were), 'I will partake of it with you.'

sections.Line 5: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject perfectly sincere, and linking (others) to him in closest union. There will be no error.

sections.Judgment: Hsiâo Kwo indicates that (in the circumstances which it implies) there will be progress and attainment. But it will be advantageous to be firm and correct. There will (in this way) be great good fortune.
sections.Line 1: The first SIX, divided, suggests (the idea of) a bird flying, (and ascending) till the issue is evil.
sections.Line 2: The second SIX, divided, shows its subject passing by his grandfather, and meeting with his grandmother; not attempting anything against his ruler, but meeting him as his minister. There will be no error.
sections.Line 3: The third NINE, undivided, shows its subject taking no extraordinary precautions against danger; and some in consequence finding opportunity to assail and injure him. There will be evil.
sections.Line 4: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows its subject falling into no error, but meeting (the exigency of his situation), without exceeding (in his natural course). If he go forward, there will be peril, and he must be cautious. There is no occasion to be using firmness perpetually.
sections.Line 5: The fifth SIX, divided, (suggests the idea) of dense clouds, but no rain, coming from our borders in the west. It also (shows) the prince shooting his arrow, and taking the bird in a cave.
sections.Line 6: The sixth SIX, divided, shows its subject not meeting (the exigency of his situation), and exceeding (his proper course). (It suggests the idea of) a bird flying far aloft. There will be evil. The case is what is called one of calamity and self-produced injury.

sections.Judgment: Kî Žî intimates progress and success in small matters. There will be advantage in being firm and correct. There has been good fortune in the beginning; there may be disorder in the end.
sections.Line 1: The first NINE, undivided, (shows its subject as a driver) who drags back his wheel, (or as a fox) which has wet his tail. There will be no error.
sections.Line 2: The second SIX, divided, (shows its subject as) a wife who has lost her (carriage-)screen. There is no occasion to go in pursuit of it. In seven days she will find it.
sections.Line 3: The third NINE, undivided, (suggests the case of) Kâo Žung, who attacked the Demon region, but was three years in subduing it. Small men should not be employed (in such enterprises).
sections.Line 4: The fourth SIX, divided, shows its subject with rags provided against any leak (in his boat), and on his guard all day long.
sections.Line 5: The fifth NINE, undivided, shows its subject (as) the neighbour in the east who slaughters an ox (for his sacrifice); but this is not equal to the (small) spring sacrifice of the neighbour in the west, whose sincerity receives the blessing.
sections.Line 6: The topmost SIX, divided, shows its subject with (even) his head immersed. The position is perilous.

sections.Judgment: Wei Žî intimates progress and success (in the circumstances which it implies). (We see) a young fox that has nearly crossed (the stream), when its tail gets immersed. There will be no advantage in any way.
sections.Line 1: The first SIX, divided, shows its subject (like a fox) whose tail gets immersed. There will be occasion for regret.
sections.Line 2: The second NINE, undivided, shows its subject dragging back his (carriage-) wheel. With firmness and correctness there will be good fortune.
sections.Line 3: The third SIX, divided, shows its subject, with (the state of things) not yet remedied, advancing on; which will lead to evil. But there will be advantage in (trying to) cross the great stream.
sections.Line 4: The fourth NINE, undivided, shows its subject by firm correctness obtaining good fortune, so that all occasion for repentance disappears. sections.Line 5: The fifth SIX, divided, shows its subject by firm correctness obtaining good fortune, and having no occasion for repentance. (We see in him) the brightness of a superior man, and the possession of sincerity. There will be good fortune.
sections.Line 6: The topmost NINE, undivided, shows its subject full of confidence and therefore feasting (quietly). There will be no error. (If he) cherish this confidence, till he (is like the fox who) gets his head immersed, it will fail of what is right.

items.name: The Ten Wings — what this layer is

sections.What it is: The Shiyi (十翼), the 'Ten Wings', are the classical commentaries bound together with the Zhouyi core to make the book we call the I Ching. They are what turned a Bronze Age divination manual into a work of philosophy: the cosmology of yin and yang, the 'superior man' who reads each hexagram as moral instruction, the whole metaphysical frame that most readers now assume IS the I Ching. This grammar holds that layer apart so you can see it as a layer — an addition, magnificent on its own terms, but not the origin. The ten are: the Tuan Zhuan in two parts (wings 1–2), the Xiang Zhuan in two parts (wings 3–4), the Xici or Great Commentary in two parts (wings 5–6), the Wenyan (wing 7), the Shuogua (wing 8), the Xugua (wing 9), and the Zagua (wing 10).
sections.Dating & authorship: Tradition credits all ten to Confucius (551–479 BCE). That attribution has been doubted at least since the Song scholar Ouyang Xiu (1007–1072) ✔, and modern scholarship rejects it: the Wings are composite works by multiple hands in the Confucian school, composed roughly between the late Warring States and the early Han — c. 350–100 BCE, several centuries after the Zhouyi core ✔ (Shaughnessy, 'I ching (Chou I)' in Early Chinese Texts; Rutt, Zhouyi: A Bronze Age Document, 1996; Redmond & Hon, Teaching the I Ching, 2014). The earliest physical witness to any Wing is the Mawangdui silk manuscript, from a tomb sealed 168 BCE, which contains a version of the Xici ✔. None of this makes the Wings lesser — it makes them legible as what they are: the moment a divination text was canonized into philosophy.

items.name: Tuan Zhuan — Commentary on the Judgments (wings 1–2)

sections.What it is: A hexagram-by-hexagram commentary on the Judgment texts, explaining each verdict through the hexagram's structure: the trigrams' imagery, which lines are strong or weak, central or correct. This is where systematic hexagram-analysis begins — the core text never explains itself; the Tuan Zhuan does, and its methods (line positions, correlates, centrality) became the grammar of all later Yijing interpretation. ○
sections.In Legge's translation (1882): On hexagram 1: "Vast is the 'great and originating (power)' indicated by Khien! All things owe to it their beginning:—it contains all the meaning belonging to (the name) heaven." (Appendix I in Legge's arrangement.) ✔

items.name: Xiang Zhuan — Commentary on the Images (wings 3–4)

sections.What it is: Two commentaries in one: the Great Images (Daxiang) — one meditation per hexagram reading the paired trigrams as a natural image and drawing a moral for the junzi, the 'superior man' — and the Small Images (Xiaoxiang), brief verse comments on each line statement. The Daxiang is the most recognizable Confucian voice in the book, and the clearest example of the moralizing layer: the old oracle says 'dragon hidden in the deep; do not act', and the Daxiang answers with what a gentleman should cultivate. The 64 hexagram items in THIS grammar carry the complete Daxiang, so you can read the moral layer straight through. ○
sections.In Legge's translation (1882): On hexagram 1: "Heaven, in its motion, (gives the idea of) strength. The superior man, in accordance with this, nerves himself to ceaseless activity." (Appendix II in Legge's arrangement.) ✔

sections.What it is: The philosophical heart of the Wings: not a hexagram-by-hexagram commentary but a treatise on what the Yi IS — how the sages made it, how change itself works, why the alternation of yin and yang is the pattern of the world. Its cosmology (the Taiji producing the two forms, the four emblems, the eight trigrams) shaped two thousand years of Chinese thought, Confucian and Daoist alike. ○ Edward Shaughnessy places its editing between about 320 and 168 BCE; a version was in the Mawangdui tomb sealed 168 BCE. ✔
sections.In Legge's translation (1882): "Therefore in (the system of) the Yî there is the Grand Terminus, which produced the two elementary Forms. Those two Forms produced the Four emblematic Symbols, which again produced the eight Trigrams." (Xici I; Legge's 'Great Appendix', Appendix III.) ✔

sections.What it is: An extended moral-philosophical meditation on the first two hexagrams only — Qian and Kun, heaven and earth — much of it framed as answers by 'the Master'. That framing is exactly how a later school writes its teacher's voice into an older text, and it is the main reason the whole book was traditionally credited to Confucius. ○

sections.What it is: A treatise on the eight trigrams: their family roles (father, mother, three sons, three daughters), compass directions, animals, body parts, and natural images. It reads like a diviner's reference distilled into scripture — much of the symbol-vocabulary later tradition treats as timeless is codified here. Parts of its material also circulated with the Xici in the Mawangdui manuscript. ○

sections.Image: Heaven's movement is full of power. Thus the superior one makes themselves strong and untiring.
sections.Line 1: Hidden creative power not yet expressed. Foundation building. Modesty in creative expression—waiting for the right timing before revealing your direction.
sections.Line 2: Emerging into view. Creative power begins to manifest. Natural creative expression that doesn't force itself but emerges when recognized.
sections.Line 3: Active all day, vigilant at night. Creative work requires sustained attention. Dedicated creativity, but watch for burnout from over-identifying with your expression.
sections.Line 4: Wavering flight, flexibility in expression. Exploring different creative directions without commitment—this is healthy experimentation.
sections.Line 5: Flying dragon in the heavens—creative power at its peak. Full, mature creative expression that influences the collective.
sections.Line 6: Arrogant dragon will have cause to repent. Over-identification with your creativity leads to rigidity. Stay humble.
sections.Judgment: The Creative works through sublime success, furthering through perseverance. What begins as pure potential becomes manifest through sustained direction.
sections.Interpretation: Gate 1 represents the archetypal force of creative self-expression and unique direction. This is the impulse to express something that only you can bring into the world. In the bodygraph, it sits in the G Center (Identity) and speaks to knowing your creative direction in life, your unique contribution, your authentic voice. When this gate is defined (activated by planets at birth), there may be a consistent pull toward expressing individuality and showing others new directions or possibilities. When undefined, there's more flexibility about creative direction, sampling different paths without fixed commitment. The classical I Ching interpretation emphasizes pure creative power—heaven doubled—suggesting relentless forward motion and the ability to initiate cycles. In Human Design's reinterpretation, this becomes personal creative authority rather than cosmic force. The energy here is about demonstrating that each person has a unique direction to offer, modeling individuality without demanding that others follow. The shadow appears when creativity is forced on demand, when expression becomes performative rather than authentic, or when the need to be unique overrides genuine self-knowing. The gift is natural self-expression that inspires without coercion—you show what's possible simply by being yourself creatively. Practically, this gate often manifests as people looking to you for creative direction, not because you're trying to lead but because your authentic expression naturally reveals new possibilities. This is symbolic language for contemplating your relationship to creative individuality, not a fixed mandate about who you must be.

sections.Image: The earth's condition is receptive devotion. Thus the superior one carries all things with spacious virtue.
sections.Line 1: Treading on hoarfrost, solid ice ahead. Early intuitive knowing—trust the small signs before direction becomes obvious.
sections.Line 2: Straight, square, great. No practice needed—natural receptivity. Your knowing is reliable without effort when you trust it.
sections.Line 3: Hidden lines keep persevering. Sometimes your direction is private—not all knowing needs to be shared immediately.
sections.Line 4: Tied-up sack—no blame, no praise. Restraint in sharing your direction. Not all inner knowing is for public consumption.
sections.Line 5: Yellow lower garment brings supreme fortune. Grounded, centered receptivity. Your direction serves others when it comes from calm presence.
sections.Line 6: Dragons fight in the meadow. Conflict between forcing direction and receiving it. Choose receptivity over ego.
sections.Judgment: The Receptive brings supreme success through the perseverance of a mare. Receptivity is not passive—it's responsive, intuitive, and profoundly generative.
sections.Interpretation: Gate 2 represents receptive knowing of direction—the counterpart to Gate 1's creative expression. This is your connection to intuitive guidance about where you're meant to go, your internal GPS for life direction. When defined, there's consistent access to inner knowing about direction. When undefined, direction is sampled from others and learned through experience. The classical I Ching's pure receptivity—earth doubled—emphasizes yielding strength, the power of allowing rather than forcing. In Human Design's framework, this becomes your capacity to receive direction from something larger than ego: intuition, higher self, synchronicity, whatever language fits your worldview. The key distinction is that this isn't passive waiting; it's responsive receptivity. You know where you're going by staying open to intuitive hits, dreams, gut feelings, or simply allowing the knowing to emerge rather than manufacturing it mentally. The shadow is forcing direction through willpower when genuine inner knowing isn't present, or spiritual bypassing where you avoid responsibility by waiting for the universe to tell you everything. The gift is trusting receptive knowing even when it doesn't make logical sense, even when you can't explain why you're going this direction. Practically, this gate often manifests as finding that your best direction comes when you stop trying to figure it out mentally and just allow the knowing to surface. Whether this reflects actual energetic wiring or is simply a useful metaphor for trusting intuition over analysis is an open question. The archetypal language can be valuable for contemplation regardless.

sections.Image: Thunder and water mix: difficulty at the beginning. The superior one brings order out of chaos.
sections.Line 1: Hesitation and hindrance. Waiting for the right moment to initiate—don't force mutation prematurely.
sections.Line 2: Difficulties pile up. Multiple new beginnings at once can be overwhelming. Focus and persevere with support.
sections.Line 3: Hunting without a guide. Innovation without direction leads to confusion. Seek guidance or collaborate.
sections.Line 4: Seeking help brings good fortune. Mutation is more successful when you involve others in the process.
sections.Line 5: Difficulties in blessing others. Your innovations may not be immediately appreciated—trust the process.
sections.Line 6: Horse and wagon part—tears flow. Sometimes new directions require leaving old forms behind. Grieve and continue.
sections.Judgment: Initial difficulty brings supreme success through perseverance. Do not undertake anything new lightly, but appointing helpers brings good fortune.
sections.Interpretation: Gate 3 in the Sacral Center represents mutation or ordering through chaos—the energy of innovation through experimentation. This is about starting new things even when you don't have all the pieces figured out, trusting that order will emerge from the initial chaos. The classical hexagram speaks to the difficulty inherent in all beginnings: thunder and water mixing creates turbulence before clarity. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes your relationship to change, novelty, and the messy process of bringing new things into form. If defined, there's consistent access to innovative energy, though it may feel chaotic or uncertain. You can handle disorder because you trust that patterns will emerge. If undefined, innovation comes in bursts or is learned from others. The shadow is forcing change just for change's sake, getting addicted to chaos, or getting stuck in perpetual experimentation without bringing things to completion. The gift is trusting the mutation process—knowing that difficulty at the beginning doesn't mean you're on the wrong path, it just means you're actually creating something new rather than repeating the known. Order emerges through the experimental process, not before it. Practically, this gate often manifests as being pulled toward experimental approaches, struggling with traditional orderly systems, and excelling when given permission to try unusual solutions. Whether this reflects actual energetic design or is simply a useful lens for understanding different approaches to innovation and change remains contemplative territory. The archetypal language serves self-reflection.

sections.Image: A spring flows from the base of the mountain: the image of youth. The superior one develops character through thorough actions.
sections.Line 1: To discipline the fool brings humiliation. Mental clarity requires experience, not force. Allow answers to emerge.
sections.Line 2: To bear with fools with kindness brings good fortune. Patience with your own and others' learning process.
sections.Line 3: Don't be like a girl who loses herself for metal and gold. Don't abandon your mental process for superficial answers.
sections.Line 4: Entangled folly brings humiliation. Getting lost in your own mental formulas without reality-testing.
sections.Line 5: Childlike folly brings good fortune. Beginner's mind—approaching problems with openness rather than fixed formulas.
sections.Line 6: Punishing folly doesn't further. Forcing mental clarity or judging confusion doesn't help. Allow understanding to unfold.
sections.Judgment: Success comes not from seeking the oracle, but from the oracle seeking you. The first time brings an answer; repeating questions shows lack of respect.
sections.Interpretation: Gate 4 in the Ajna Center represents the process of forming mental formulas, answers, and logical frameworks. This is about your relationship to mental certainty and conceptual organization. In the classical I Ching, 'youthful folly' refers to the inexperienced mind that asks questions without yet understanding how to evaluate answers. In Human Design's reinterpretation, this becomes whether you have consistent access to mental clarity and formulization. If defined, there's a reliable way of arriving at conclusions and creating frameworks. You might be the person others come to for answers. If undefined, thinking is more fluid and open to multiple perspectives without needing certainty. The classical wisdom here is about respecting the process of learning: don't ask the same question repeatedly expecting different answers. Form your answer, test it, revise it based on results. The shadow is either getting stuck in rigid mental formulas ('this IS the answer') or drowning in uncertainty because you can't commit to any framework. The gift is mental clarity that serves others—not because your formulas are objectively correct, but because they're coherent enough to be useful. Your frameworks help organize complexity into workable patterns. Practically, this gate often manifests as naturally systematizing information, creating frameworks, or developing formulas (mathematical, philosophical, practical) that help make sense of complex data. Remember that this speaks to mental processing style, not intelligence or correctness. Different ways of thinking have different gifts.

sections.Image: Clouds rise up to heaven: the image of waiting. The superior one eats, drinks, and remains serene.
sections.Line 1: Waiting in the meadow. Patience in familiar territory. Your natural rhythms are reliable when you honor them.
sections.Line 2: Waiting on the sand—gossip emerges. Disruptions to your rhythm may cause irritability. Stay grounded.
sections.Line 3: Waiting in mud invites danger. Fighting against your natural rhythms leads to depletion.
sections.Line 4: Waiting in blood—get out of the pit. Crisis forces adaptation. Fixed rhythms must sometimes flex.
sections.Line 5: Waiting at meat and drink. Trust that nourishment comes when you honor your timing.
sections.Line 6: Fall into the pit—unexpected guests arrive. Disruption of rhythms can bring unexpected gifts if you remain open.
sections.Judgment: Waiting with confidence brings supreme success. Perseverance furthers. Crossing the great water is favorable.
sections.Interpretation: Gate 5 in the Sacral Center represents fixed rhythms and natural patterns of consistency. This is about your relationship to habit, routine, and regular patterns in life. The classical I Ching hexagram emphasizes waiting with confidence—not anxious waiting, but patient trust that the right timing will emerge. Water above heaven suggests nourishment that will come in its natural time. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes about your body's natural rhythms: sleep, hunger, work cycles, creative flow. If this gate is defined in your Sacral, there's a consistent daily rhythm that works well—disrupting it causes depletion. You might naturally wake at the same time, need meals at regular intervals, or have predictable energy patterns. If undefined, there's more flexibility with timing and rhythms, adapting easily to changing schedules. The shadow is rigidity—forcing yourself or others to conform to a fixed pattern even when life requires flexibility. Or conversely, fighting against your natural rhythms because they seem boring or limiting. The gift is honoring consistent patterns without making them an identity or prison. You can have a morning routine and still adapt when needed. The structure serves you; you don't serve the structure. Practically, this gate often manifests as thriving with regular schedules and predictability. Travel, irregular hours, or chaos might be more depleting than for others. Whether this reflects actual energetic wiring or is a useful framework for understanding individual differences in need for consistency versus variety remains an open question for contemplation.

sections.Image: Heaven and water move in opposite directions: the image of conflict. The superior one carefully considers the beginning when undertaking affairs.
sections.Line 1: Don't perpetuate conflict. Not all emotional friction needs to be pursued. Let small tensions dissolve.
sections.Line 2: Withdrawing from conflict brings no blame. Sometimes the best response to friction is stepping back.
sections.Line 3: Feed on ancient virtue—danger but good fortune in the end. Draw on past emotional wisdom when navigating current friction.
sections.Line 4: Cannot carry on the conflict—returning brings good fortune. Know when to release emotional negotiation and accept difference.
sections.Line 5: Going to court brings supreme good fortune. Formal negotiation of emotional friction (therapy, mediation) can be healing.
sections.Line 6: Even if granted a belt, it will be taken away three times before morning. Winning emotional conflicts doesn't lead to lasting intimacy.
sections.Judgment: Conflict requires seeking the middle way. Going to the source brings clarity, but pushing forward brings misfortune.
sections.Interpretation: Gate 6 in the Solar Plexus Center represents friction in intimacy—the necessary negotiation that happens when two people (or parts of yourself) have different emotional truths. This isn't conflict for conflict's sake, but the honest friction required to find authentic alignment. The classical hexagram shows heaven and water moving in opposite directions, suggesting inherent tension. In Human Design's reading, this becomes about emotional negotiation: how do you handle friction in intimate relationships? If defined in your emotional solar plexus, there's consistent energy for working through emotional friction. You might actually be comfortable with conflict as a doorway to deeper intimacy. If undefined, you might avoid friction or feel overwhelmed by emotional tension. The shadow is either forcing conflict unnecessarily (friction addiction) or suppressing genuine friction and pretending everything is fine. Neither extreme serves intimacy. The gift is recognizing that friction is how intimate systems find authentic alignment—not through pretending to agree, but through honest negotiation of different truths. You're willing to experience the discomfort of disagreement because you trust it leads somewhere real. Practically, this gate often manifests as close relationships involving substantial honest conflict. You might say 'we fight a lot but we're really close' and mean it positively. The friction builds intimacy rather than destroying it. The challenge is distinguishing productive friction (leading to deeper understanding) from destructive conflict (just causing harm). This is contemplative territory for exploring your relationship to emotional honesty in intimacy.

sections.Image: Water in the earth: the army's image. The superior one increases their masses by generous treatment of the people.
sections.Line 1: Army marches forth in order—if not orderly, misfortune. Leadership requires clear internal structure before influencing others.
sections.Line 2: In the midst of the army—good fortune, no blame. Leading from within the group rather than above it.
sections.Line 3: Army carries corpses—misfortune. Taking on others' emotional baggage while leading drains your direction.
sections.Line 4: Army retreats—no blame. Sometimes the right leadership move is withdrawal or redirection.
sections.Line 5: Field has game—advantage in capturing it. Clear purpose makes your leadership effective and beneficial.
sections.Line 6: Great prince gives commands. Mature leadership that empowers others rather than controlling them.
sections.Judgment: The army needs perseverance and a strong leader. Good fortune with no blame.
sections.Interpretation: Gate 7 in the G Center represents your role in leading or influencing others. The classical I Ching uses military metaphor: an army requires clear direction and responsible leadership. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes about your identity in relation to others—what role do you naturally play in collective settings? Are you a director, a guide, a democratic leader, or someone who prefers not to lead at all? If this gate is defined, there's consistent energy for taking a role in influencing or directing others. People might naturally look to you for guidance or expect you to take charge. If undefined, you're more flexible about roles and might not feel called to lead. The shadow is either forcing yourself into leadership when it's not your natural expression, or abdicating all responsibility for influence when you actually do have something valuable to contribute. The gift is recognizing that leadership isn't about domination; it's about clear direction that serves the collective. You know your role, you play it well, and you don't inflate or deflate its importance. You lead when appropriate and follow when appropriate, without making either an identity. Practically, this gate often manifests as finding yourself in guiding roles—not necessarily formal authority, but informal influence. You're the friend everyone comes to for direction, the colleague who naturally organizes projects, the family member who provides orientation. This is contemplative territory for exploring your relationship to influence and collective roles.

sections.Image: Water flows over earth: the image of holding together. Ancient kings established states and maintained connection with feudal lords.
sections.Line 1: Hold to them with truth—no blame. Your contribution begins with authenticity, not performance.
sections.Line 2: Hold to them from within—perseverance brings good fortune. Genuine self-expression, not manufactured image.
sections.Line 3: Hold to those who are not the right people. Trying to model for an audience that doesn't resonate with your authenticity.
sections.Line 4: Hold to them openly—perseverance brings good fortune. Public modeling of your authentic way.
sections.Line 5: Manifestation of holding together—the king uses beaters on three sides only. Your contribution attracts naturally; you don't chase an audience.
sections.Line 6: Holding together brings no head—misfortune. Contribution without authentic center becomes performative and draining.
sections.Judgment: Holding together brings good fortune. Seek the oracle again to know if you have constancy and perseverance. Then no blame.
sections.Interpretation: Gate 8 in the Throat Center represents contribution through authentic self-expression and modeling. This is about whether you make your unique contribution by demonstrating what's possible through your own example. The classical I Ching hexagram emphasizes union and holding together—water on earth creates cohesion. In Human Design's reinterpretation, this becomes about your relationship to being a role model or example. If this gate is defined in your Throat (the center of manifestation and expression), there's consistent energy for contributing by being yourself authentically and letting others learn from what you model. You're not teaching directly; you're inspiring by example. If undefined, you might contribute in other ways or be more private about your process. The shadow is performing authenticity (trying to be a role model without actually being authentic), or hiding your gifts because you don't want the visibility that comes with modeling. The gift is realizing that your authentic expression naturally contributes to the collective—you don't have to force it or manufacture it. When you're genuinely yourself, others learn something simply from witnessing your unique way of being. You contribute through honest self-expression, not through trying to set an example. Practically, this gate often manifests as feeling energized by visibility and authenticity, even when uncomfortable. You might be the friend whose honesty gives others permission to be honest, or the colleague whose unique approach opens possibilities for the team. The contemplative question is about your relationship to visibility, modeling, and contribution through authentic being.

sections.Image: Wind moves across heaven: taming power of the small. The superior one refines the outward aspect of their character.
sections.Line 1: Return to the way. How could this be a mistake? Good fortune. Focus returns to fundamentals before proceeding.
sections.Line 2: Allowing oneself to be drawn into returning. Good fortune. Focus sustained through gentle re-engagement.
sections.Line 3: The spokes burst from the wagon wheels. Man and wife turn eyes away. Focus scattered by competing demands.
sections.Line 4: If sincere, blood vanishes and fear gives way. No blame. Authentic focus dissolves obstacles.
sections.Line 5: If sincere and loyally attached, you are rich in your neighbor. Focused attention creates mutual abundance.
sections.Line 6: The rain comes, there is rest. Due to lasting effect of character. Focus sustained brings breakthrough.
sections.Judgment: The taming power of the small has success. Dense clouds but no rain from the western region.
sections.Interpretation: Gate 9 in the Sacral Center represents the power of focus on details—the capacity to concentrate life force energy on small, specific elements that accumulate into larger patterns. This isn't about missing the forest for the trees; it's about recognizing that forests are made of individual trees, each deserving attention. The classical hexagram shows wind gathering clouds without yet producing rain—potential building through patient accumulation of small elements. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes your relationship to detailed focus: can you sustain attention on specifics without losing sight of the whole? If this gate is defined in your Sacral, there's consistent energy for detailed work. You might be the person who notices what others miss, who can work with sustained attention on seemingly minor elements, who finds meaning in precision. If undefined, your focus tends toward the general or big picture, learning about detail orientation from others. The shadow appears when detail focus becomes perfectionism, when attention to small things masks avoidance of larger challenges, or when you get so lost in specifics that synthesis becomes impossible. The gift is precision that serves purpose—you can zoom in without losing perspective, attend to particulars while maintaining awareness of how they fit into wholes. You recognize that breakthrough often emerges from careful attention to what seems small rather than grasping for the dramatic. Practically, this gate often manifests as natural ability for detailed work, enjoyment of tasks others find tedious, and capacity to find patterns in specifics. Whether this reflects actual energetic wiring or is useful metaphor for different cognitive styles remains contemplative territory.

sections.Image: Heaven above, the lake below: treading. The superior one discriminates between high and low and thereby fortifies the thinking of the people.
sections.Line 1: Simple conduct. Progress without blame. Behavior flows from authentic simplicity.
sections.Line 2: Treading a smooth level course. Perseverance brings good fortune. Steady authentic behavior.
sections.Line 3: A one-eyed person can see, a lame person can tread. Steps on tiger's tail—it bites. Behavior overreaching capacity.
sections.Line 4: Steps on tiger's tail. Caution and circumspection lead to ultimate good fortune. Authentic but careful conduct.
sections.Line 5: Resolute conduct. Perseverance with awareness of danger. Bold authentic behavior with eyes open.
sections.Line 6: Look to your conduct and weigh the favorable signs. Supreme good fortune. Self-reflective authentic behavior.
sections.Judgment: Treading upon the tail of the tiger—it does not bite. Success.
sections.Interpretation: Gate 10 in the G Center represents behavior of the self—how you naturally conduct yourself in the world, your authentic way of being that comes from self-love rather than performance. The classical hexagram suggests treading carefully in dangerous places, walking the tiger's tail without getting bitten through proper conduct. In Human Design's framework, this becomes about whether your behavior flows from genuine self-acceptance or from trying to be what you think you should be. If this gate is defined in your G Center, there's consistent energy for authentic self-conduct. You might be someone who naturally behaves in ways that feel true to yourself, even when unconventional. Your behavior isn't calculated for effect; it emerges from self-love. If undefined, your behavior is more flexible and adaptive, learning different modes of conduct from various situations and people. The shadow appears when behavior becomes performance—when you're so focused on conducting yourself 'correctly' that authenticity disappears, or when self-love hardens into narcissism where only your way is valid. The gift is natural authenticity—your behavior reflects genuine self-acceptance, which paradoxically makes it easier for others to be authentic around you. You tread carefully not from fear but from respect for both yourself and others. You can be fully yourself without trampling on others' right to be themselves. Practically, this gate often shows up as people saying 'you're always so yourself' or 'I can be myself around you.' Whether this reflects energetic design or useful language for self-acceptance remains open for contemplation.

sections.Image: Heaven and earth unite: the image of peace. The sovereign divides and completes the course of heaven and earth.
sections.Line 1: When ribbon grass is pulled up, the sod comes with it. Each according to their kind. Undertakings bring good fortune. Ideas emerge in clusters.
sections.Line 2: Bearing with the uncultured in gentleness, fording the river with resolution. Ideas require both openness and determination.
sections.Line 3: No plain not followed by a slope. No going not followed by a return. Ideas cycle naturally.
sections.Line 4: Flutters down, not boasting of wealth, together with neighbors. Ideas shared create community.
sections.Line 5: The sovereign gives his daughter in marriage. This brings blessing and supreme good fortune. Ideas find perfect implementation.
sections.Line 6: The city wall falls back into the moat. Use no army now. Ideas dissolve back into potential when their time passes.
sections.Judgment: Peace. The small departs, the great approaches. Good fortune. Success.
sections.Interpretation: Gate 11 in the Ajna Center represents ideas and concepts—the mental capacity to receive and generate abstract thoughts that may or may not have immediate practical application. The classical hexagram shows heaven and earth in harmonious union, suggesting that peace emerges when higher and lower, abstract and concrete, find alignment. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes your relationship to ideas: do you have consistent access to conceptual thinking, or is your mind more focused on immediate practical matters? If this gate is defined in your Ajna, there's regular energy for idea generation. You might be someone who has lots of ideas, who lives partly in the realm of concepts, who can think abstractly with ease. People might come to you for new perspectives or unusual angles. If undefined, your thinking is more grounded in what's immediately relevant, learning about abstract ideation from others. The shadow is either idea addiction (so many concepts that nothing gets implemented) or getting lost in mental realms disconnected from embodied reality. The gift is idea generation that serves life—you can think conceptually without losing touch with what matters on the ground. Your ideas create peace rather than confusion because they help people see new possibilities without demanding they abandon practical wisdom. Practically, this gate often manifests as being 'the idea person' in groups, having insights that seem to come from nowhere, or finding that your best contribution is conceptual rather than implementation-focused. This is contemplative territory for exploring how abstract thinking serves lived experience.

sections.Image: Heaven and earth do not unite: the image of standstill. The superior one falls back upon their inner worth to escape difficulties.
sections.Line 1: When ribbon grass is pulled up, the sod comes with it. Perseverance brings good fortune and success. Cautious withdrawal from premature expression.
sections.Line 2: They bear and endure; this means good fortune for inferior people. The standstill serves success of the great one. Caution as service.
sections.Line 3: They bear shame. Recognition that the time for expression hasn't arrived.
sections.Line 4: One who acts at the command of the highest remains without blame. Cautious expression under proper authority.
sections.Line 5: Standstill is giving way. Good fortune for the great one. What if it should fail? Caution relaxing as timing shifts.
sections.Line 6: The standstill comes to an end. First standstill, then good fortune. Caution gives way to expression.
sections.Judgment: Standstill. Evil people do not further the perseverance of the superior one. The great departs; the small approaches.
sections.Interpretation: Gate 12 in the Throat Center represents caution in expression—knowing when to speak and when to remain silent, when to articulate what you know and when to wait for right timing. The classical hexagram shows heaven and earth separated, communication blocked, suggesting that sometimes standstill is the appropriate response rather than forced movement. In Human Design's reading, this becomes your relationship to expressing yourself: do you have consistent access to knowing when to speak versus when to pause? If this gate is defined in your Throat, there's regular energy for discerning right timing of expression. You might be someone who knows when words will land versus when they'll fall on deaf ears, who can hold back expression when the moment isn't ripe. If undefined, your expression is more spontaneous or learned situationally from others. The shadow appears when caution becomes suppression (never speaking up) or when timing-awareness becomes manipulation (withholding strategically for effect). The gift is wise restraint that serves communication—you know that not everything that can be said should be said, and not every moment is the right moment. Your caution isn't fear; it's respect for the power of words and awareness of readiness in listeners. Practically, this gate often manifests as being told 'you always know the right time to say things' or finding that when you do speak after waiting, people really hear you. This is contemplative territory about the relationship between silence and speech.

sections.Image: Heaven together with fire: the image of fellowship. The superior one organizes clans and makes distinctions between things.
sections.Line 1: Fellowship at the gate. No blame. Listening begins with open invitation.
sections.Line 2: Fellowship with people in the clan. Humiliation. Listening constrained by tribe rather than open.
sections.Line 3: Hides weapons in the thicket. Climbs the high hill. For three years does not rise up. Listening blocked by suspicion.
sections.Line 4: Climbs up on their wall but cannot attack. Good fortune. Listening that maintains boundaries.
sections.Line 5: People bound in fellowship first weep and lament, but afterward they laugh. After great struggles they succeed in meeting. Deep listening through difficulty.
sections.Line 6: Fellowship in the meadow. No remorse. Listening that creates open community.
sections.Judgment: Fellowship with others in the open. Success. It furthers one to cross the great water. Perseverance of the superior one furthers.
sections.Interpretation: Gate 13 in the G Center represents the listener—the capacity to hear and hold others' stories, secrets, and experiences, to serve as witness to what people need to express. The classical hexagram emphasizes fellowship in the open, suggesting that genuine community emerges when people can share openly with those who truly listen. In Human Design's interpretation, this becomes whether you have consistent energy for deep listening and holding space for others' expression. If this gate is defined in your G Center, there's regular capacity for listening without needing to fix, judge, or redirect. You might be the person people naturally confide in, who can hear difficult truths without collapsing or rejecting. Your listening creates fellowship because people feel genuinely met. If undefined, you learn about deep listening from others and may be more focused on your own expression. The shadow appears when listening becomes passive reception without boundaries, when you're so busy holding others' stories that you lose your own voice, or when 'being a good listener' becomes an identity that prevents authentic relationship. The gift is generative listening—your capacity to hear others actually helps them hear themselves. You don't just receive; your listening creates space for people to discover what they really need to say. Practically, this gate often shows up as 'I don't know why I'm telling you this' or people feeling understood in your presence. This is contemplative territory about the power of being witnessed.

sections.Image: Fire in heaven above: possession in great measure. The superior one curbs evil and furthers good, obedient to the benevolent will of heaven.
sections.Line 1: No relationship with what is harmful. No blame. Blameless if one remains conscious of difficulty. Power used consciously.
sections.Line 2: A big wagon for loading. One may undertake something. No blame. Power can carry weight.
sections.Line 3: A prince offers it to the Son of Heaven. A petty person cannot do this. Power shared with those worthy.
sections.Line 4: Makes no mistake in distinguishing from neighbor. No blame. Power discerning in application.
sections.Line 5: Whose truth is accessible yet dignified obtains good fortune. Power combined with authenticity.
sections.Line 6: Is blessed by heaven. Good fortune. Nothing that does not further. Power blessed by alignment.
sections.Judgment: Possession in great measure. Supreme success.
sections.Interpretation: Gate 14 in the Sacral Center represents power skills—the capacity to develop and wield resources, whether material, energetic, or skillful, and to do so in service of something meaningful.
